results.title: I can't believe PowerShell is good
results.author: Corbin Davenport
results.content:
Microsoft makes a lot of bad software. That includes many aspects of Windows, from the primary email application being a web wrapper to the ever-present Copilot buttons. As such, it's always a surprise to me when I find a Microsoft product that improves my life in some respect, especially when it's something that came from Windows.
I never paid much attention to PowerShell, the command-line shell and scripting tool that first arrived in 2006, and became a bundled application with the release of Windows 7. For the time period I used Windows as my main desktop operating system, I mostly stuck to the Command Prompt and Batch scripts, or Bash in WSL or Python for more complex tasks. The modern version of PowerShell is cross-platform, and can also be installed on Mac and Linux.
Earlier this year, I needed to learn PowerShell scripting for one Windows-related project, and I have tried it out a few more times on Mac. It has quickly become one of my favorite tools for automation and scripting—taking on jobs that I would have otherwise tried to do with Node.js, Shortcuts, macOS Automator, or heaven forbid, Bash scripts.
I get it now. PowerShell is great, even if you don't use it as your shell, and even if you're on Mac or Linux.
Bashing my head against the wall
The most common way to run a sequence of commands on Linux, macOS, and other Unix-based environments is with a Bash script. They are also called shell scripts, even though they're not technically the same thing, because they are also used by other shells like Z Shell (zsh).
Here's an example Bash script that asks you for a media URL, and then uses the yt-dlp application to save it as an MP3 audio file to your Desktop folder:
#!/bin/bash
echo -e "Enter a URL: "
read url
cd ~/Desktop
yt-dlp -x --audio-format mp3 "$url"
echo "Done!"
Bash scripts are fine for just running a series of commands. You can use variables and loops, code you use more than once can go in a function, and there's even limited support for data types like arrays. They can also sometimes work on a wide variety of hardware and operating systems.
For anything slightly more complicated, Bash scripting is just the worst. There are almost no "built-in" functions—you are supposed to use POSIX commands for common tasks, like file operations or parsing text. Anything beyond that depends on external tools, like cURL or Wget for retrieving web content, several different applications for accessing the clipboard, and jq for reading JSON data. You might also need boilerplate code for parsing options and parameters.
It is also surprisingly difficult to make a Bash script that works reliably on other people's computers. Some people might try your script in a different shell that doesn't interpret scripts in the same way—that's why the command for installing Homebrew starts with calling the bash shell specifically, and many other tools use the same trick. Someone might only have cURL installed for fetching web content, or only Wget, or both, or neither! You can't assume every system will have the same basic set of POSIX commands, or even the sudo command, as I learned a few months ago.
The limitations of Bash scripting usually pushed me towards actual programming languages, even for tasks that didn't strictly need them. Python might be the best alternative, but its lack of curly braces makes me sad. I write a lot of JavaScript code, so Node.js is an option, but I have to put await operators everywhere for system operations and hope that I'm not installing malware when more dependencies are needed.
Hello, PowerShell
Like many other products from Microsoft (and Google), PowerShell is actually two different things with similar names. The one you should use is PowerShell 7, also called PowerShell Core, which is the modern cross-platform version based on .NET Core. The other one is Windows PowerShell (v5.1 and below), which is based on .NET Framework and not actively developed. Windows 11 still only includes Windows PowerShell, and not PowerShell 7.
PowerShell 7 is a free download on Windows, Mac, and Linux. On my Mac computers, I used Homebrew to install it, and then I can run it with pwsh in the Terminal.
The basic premise of a PowerShell script isn't much different than a Bash script. It's a list of commands, either provided by the shell or the underlying system, with the ability to use additional functions and keywords (like if, foreach, or try/catch) as needed.
PowerShell has many built-in commands, called "cmdlets" (pronounced "command-lets"), and you can install more or make your own. The names for most of them are verb-noun pairs, like Set-Location instead of POSIX's cd, Clear-Host instead of cls, and Remove-Item instead of rm.
Here's that MP3 downloader again, but now as a PowerShell script:
Param(
    [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)][uri]$url
)
Set-Location -Path ~/Desktop
yt-dlp -x --audio-format mp3 "$url"
Write-Host "Done!"
The cool part in that script is the Param block, which uses PowerShell's built-in parameter support to define "url" as a mandatory URI input. PowerShell will ask for that URL when the script starts, similar to the Bash example, while also allowing a -url parameter on the script as an alternative input method.
You can even run PowerShell's built-in Get-Help command on the script, which shows the list of parameters with their data types, just like Get-Help would for a built-in command.
This same functionality in Bash would need a lot of boilerplate code with getparams and various if statements. PowerShell handles all that for you.
In case you were wondering, that Unix-style ~/Desktop path works in PowerShell on all platforms. Even though Windows uses paths with backslashes at the system level, PowerShell can convert them as needed—native system commands might not, though, unless you use the Convert-Path cmdlet first. Just like in Bash, the tilde (~) character is an alias for the home directory, or you can use the $HOME variable that PowerShell supports on all platforms.
PowerShell has native support for integers, strings, arrays, and hash tables. That's especially useful when parsing content from web APIs, because PowerShell can convert to and from JSON. It's also fully object-oriented, and you can create custom objects or call .NET functions if needed.
You can use any text editor to write PowerShell scripts, just like with Bash. If you happen to use Visual Studio Code, it offers syntax completions, definition tracking, and linting support for PowerShell, among other features.
The trial run
My first real project with PowerShell was Just the Browser, a project that aims to remove AI features, tracking, and other unwanted functionality from desktop web browsers. The installer for Mac and Linux is a Bash script, so it made sense to make the Windows version as a PowerShell script.
The installer's job is to check which browsers are present on the computer, and then show an "Update settings" menu item for each browser. When that item is selected, the script downloads and installs a Windows registry file containing the browser settings. If the settings have been installed, the script shows an additional "Remove settings" option in the menu to reverse the process.
This works by creating a list object with a .NET List<T> Class, with each list item being an object that contains a menu label and update/remove function. To check if any registry entries have already been modified, I used the Test-Path and Get-ItemProperty cmdlets, like this:
if (Test-Path "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Google\Chrome") {
  $IfAiSettingExists = (Get-ItemProperty -Path "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Google\Chrome").AIModeSettings
}
There are a few cool things in that snippet. You might have noticed that registry path looks more like a file path on a drive called "HKLM" than the usual Windows Registry hierarchy, which looks like this:
HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Google\Chrome
PowerShell creates a virtual drive for the Windows Registry, allowing you to get, add, change, clear, and delete registry keys as if they were files in any file system. That same Test-Path cmdlet would also work for checking if a certain file was in my Downloads folder. You don't have to learn how to use files and how to use registry keys, because they're the same thing in PowerShell.
There are other virtual drives in PowerShell, like the one for certificate storage in Windows, and you can even create your own. If you're tired of typing a long path in your shell or scripts, make a virtual drive that points to it! You can even call it FART:\ if you want.
That script also has to download the .reg files for configuring web browsers. Here's a simplified version of the process for Google Chrome:
$GoogleChromeInstallRegistry = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/corbindavenport/just-the-browser/main/chrome/install.reg"
Invoke-WebRequest $GoogleChromeInstallRegistry -OutFile "$env:LocalAppData\chrome.reg"
$ChromeInstall = Start-Process "reg.exe" -ArgumentList "import `"$env:LocalAppData\chrome.reg`"" -WindowStyle Hidden -Wait -PassThru
This uses the Invoke-WebRequest cmdlet to download the registry file from the provided URL, and stores it temporarily in the user account's AppData folder. It then starts the reg.exe command in a hidden window, tells it to import the file that was just downloaded, and waits until the command is completed. PowerShell could modify the keys directly, but I wanted them to be in a separate file that can be imported manually, since not everyone wants to use the automated installer.
The Invoke-WebRequest cmdlet works like Wget or cURL on a Mac or Linux system, allowing you to download web content in your script. That's another feature built into PowerShell on all platforms that I frequently need in Bash scripts.
curl command that redirected to Invoke-WebRequest. It didn't support all the same features as cURL, which led to people filing bug reports for the actual cURL project. That alias was removed in PowerShell 7, and Windows now includes the real application.
I wanted the installer to work in older versions of Windows PowerShell, so it could run on older PCs without first upgrading the PowerShell version. That only required a few alterations, like this command that enables TLS v1.2 before using Invoke-WebRequest, because it used to not be enabled by default:
[Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol=[Net.SecurityProtocolType]::Tls12
For another project, I was experimenting with merging my old Tumblr blog into my main personal website, which uses the Eleventy static site generator. There were no existing tools for that, so I created a "Tumblr to Eleventy" PowerShell script.
The script has two main inputs: Tumblr's archive export, which is a bunch of HTML and media attachments in a ZIP file, and the Tumblr API. It uses Invoke-WebRequest and ConvertFrom-Json to check the API and iterate through all posts on the blog, Expand-Archive to extract the ZIP file, and cmdlets like Copy-Item and New-Item to create a new file structure ready for an Eleventy site.
The most important part was keeping all the metadata from the original Tumblr post, including the title, permalink, publish date, and tags. The script does that by creating a custom object with all the data, then turns it into Eleventy-friendly JSON format with the ConvertTo-Json cmdlet:
$OutputJson = Join-Path -Path $OutputPath -ChildPath "index.json"
$PostMetadata = [PSCustomObject]@{
    title = $Post.title ? $Post.title : $Post.summary
    permalink = ($Post.post_url -replace $Post.blog.url, "/") + "/index.html"
    date = [DateTimeOffset]::FromUnixTimeSeconds($Post.timestamp).UtcDateTime.ToString("yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm:ssZ")
    tags = $tag ? (@($tag) + $Post.tags) : $Post.tags
    tumblr_id = $Post.id
    tumblr_url = $Post.post_url
    tumblr_short_url = $Post.short_url
    tumblr_blog_name = $Post.blog_name
}
$PostMetadata | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 1 | Set-Content -Path $OutputJson -Encoding UTF8
The $Post variable contains the response from the Tumblr API, so this is just mapping that data to the keys that Eleventy expects. For example, the API sometimes put my post titles as the summary instead of the title, so the script checks .title first and uses .summary as the fallback. Tumblr provided the publish date and time for each post in Unix time, which PowerShell can convert to the UTC format required by Eleventy.
I probably would have used Node.js for this if it wasn't PowerShell, since Node does have built-in web requests and file handling. However, it would have needed external dependencies for simple tasks like unzipping the archive (either calling the system's unzip or using a JS-native library), as well as await statements all over the place. I didn't end up moving my blog, but hopefully someone else will find that script useful.
Another tool in the toolbox
I'm still getting the hang of PowerShell scripting, but I have come away more impressed with it after every project. It's cross-platform, more predictable and reusable than Bash scripts, and relatively easy to understand. I can't believe this came out of the same company as Copilot.
Of course, none of this matters if you do scripting and automation the cool way, with Claude or another AI chatbot taking the wheel. The bot can do the thinking and testing for you. However, I like learning things, and I'm trying my best to prevent my brain from atrophying. A local Gemma 4 model in LM Studio did help me with troubleshooting when web searches failed, but the vast majority of my scripting thus far has been lovingly hand-crafted.
If you're interested in learning how to use PowerShell, there are plenty of online guides and video tutorials. I have been watching "PowerShell 7 for Beginners" from JackedProgrammer, and I might even get a reference book at some point. It can go right next to my 1996 paperback edition of O'Reilly's HTML: The Definitive Guide.
results.summary:
Microsoft’s PowerShell 7 has emerged as a powerful, cross-platform automation tool that offers a more reliable and feature-rich alternative to traditional Bash scripting for developers and system administrators.

### Key Points
- PowerShell 7, also known as PowerShell Core, is a free, open-source tool compatible with Windows, macOS, and Linux.
- Unlike Bash, PowerShell is object-oriented and includes native support for data types like JSON, hash tables, and arrays.
- The tool utilizes "cmdlets"—standardized verb-noun commands—to perform complex tasks like file management and registry manipulation.
- PowerShell features built-in parameter handling and documentation support, reducing the need for the boilerplate code often required in shell scripts.
- It integrates seamlessly with Visual Studio Code, providing developers with syntax completion, linting, and debugging capabilities.
- Virtual drives allow users to interact with system components like the Windows Registry or certificate stores as if they were standard file systems.

### Why it Matters
PowerShell provides a consistent, robust environment for automation that eliminates many of the compatibility headaches associated with traditional Unix-based shell scripts. By offering a unified syntax across different operating systems, it simplifies complex workflows and reduces reliance on external dependencies or fragmented POSIX commands.

results.title: Can Germany overhaul its economy before AfD grows stronger?
results.author: Nik Martin
results.content:
Germany's export-led economic model faces unprecedented strain just as support for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party reaches a new peak.
Chinese rivals are steadily eroding the market share of major German industrial players, while persistently high energy prices, elevated labor costs and excessive red tape are adding to the structural crisis.
After two years of contraction, real GDP edged up only 0.2% last year, according to the Federal Statistical Office, Destatis. Exports to China fell 9.7% in 2025, withGerman vehicle and part shipments plunging by a third.
While there are signs the German economy is turning the corner, the government's latest forecast of 1.3% growth in 2026 is still modest compared with the pre-COVID boom years.
The AfD is currently polling ahead of all other political parties in Germany. The country's many economic challenges have been a major factor in the right-wing populists' rise.
Germany's domestic intelligence agency sees reliable indications that the AfD is right-wing extremist in its entirety.
The party has vowed to put Germany back on a growth path by ending the transition to renewable energies, lowering taxes and renegotiating European Union treaties, while also reforming welfare and sharply restricting immigration.
Merz seeks growth via advanced tech
As Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coalition searches for a fresh growth strategy to fend off the rise in populist politics, the government has set out its high-tech agenda focusing on six priority sectors.
These are artificial intelligence (AI), quantum computing, microelectronics, biotechnology, clean energy (including nuclear fusion) and climate-neutral mobility.
Irene Bertschek, head of the Digital Economy research unit at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW), argues that Germany's research in these "key enabling technologies is very strong, particularly in the area of climate-neutral technologies."
Yet, the results are often commercialized abroad, Bertschek told DW, with the United States leading in AI and China closing the gap quickly.
Trillions in new investments
A report published Monday by the Made for Germany initiative — a group of 147 companies and investors — builds on the government's plan, estimating that these and other new technologies could attract up to €4.1 trillion ($4.6 trillion) in investment by 2035.
Realizing that potential, however, will depend less on today's industrial giants, like Volkswagen, Siemens and BASF.
"It will not primarily be the established companies that conquer these new fields, but innovative newcomers — startups," Oliver Falck, director of the ifo Center for the Economics of Innovation and Digital Transformation, told DW.
The task, Falck said, is to create the right conditions for startups to emerge, including proximity to top universities, access to private capital and enough freedom to experiment.
He argues for state financing during the early-stage "valley of death" — the risky phase between research and commercial viability when private financing is often scarce.
Investors circle future growth sectors
There are clear signs this shift is already happening. Data from Deutsche Bank and startupdetector, a German startup database and market intelligence platform, show more than 3,000 startups were founded in Germany in the first half of 2026, up 88% from the same period last year. One-third of the new ventures have an AI focus.
Venture-capital investment soared 44% to €5.8 billion in the first half of 2026, with firms such as Neura Robotics and drone manufacturers Stark and Quantum Systems benefiting.
US investors, meanwhile, are increasingly buying up Germany's famed Mittelstand — its traditional small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) — with an eye on their specialized technology.
"The German Mittelstand is highly innovative. Now it is essential to invest in key technologies such as artificial intelligence and to tap into the potential that arises at the intersection with established technologies," Bertschek stressed.
The expert, who is also chair of the German government's Commission of Experts for Research and Innovation (EFI), thinks SMEs should make better use of their huge amounts of production data and collaborate with AI startups to help those young firms grow.
A case for special economic zones
Another idea for accelerating the shift to new high-tech sectors comes from Sven Gabor Janszky, chairman of the Leipzig-based futures-research institute 2b AHEAD. He argues that Germany needs special economic zones to help catch the next wave of economic growth.
"For a few specific technologies, you lower the regulations, you recruit ambitious workers and pump money into these zones," Janszky told DW.
This, he added, would follow the examples of Silicon Valley and Chinese mega-cities Shenzhen and Shanghai's Pudong district, and echoes the conditions that helped rebuild the German economy after World War II.
In Janszky's view, these zones would help Germany position itself as a first mover in emerging fields rather than remaining tied to older industrial strengths.
"EU regulations may try to prohibit this move, but Germany will have to overcome them so we can grow the economy again," he added.
Defense spending powers tech growth
The sharp rise in Germany's defense spending will also help several of the high-tech sectors now being prioritized.
According to the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), the defense budget is expected to reach around €120 billion in 2026 — roughly 2.6% of GDP. The government wants this figure to hit 3.5% by 2029.
The resulting procurement will provide a major boost to the production of drones, sensors, communications systems and other dual-use technologies that have both civilian and military applications.
The cost gap need not be decisive
Yet, with major rival China benefiting from much lower energy and worker costs, along with huge government subsidies, Germany will continue to face similar price disadvantages when exporting its new high-end tech. But that doesn't have to spell failure, said Falck, the ifo expert.
"Take the semiconductor industry as an example. It is probably unrealistic to aim for leadership along the entire value chain. But it is enough to lead at individual choke points," he pointed out.
"And that is exactly where Germany is strong: as a supplier of equipment for state-of-the-art chip fabs and as a supplier to the world's AI gigafactories, with power semiconductors."
In other words, with a first-mover advantage, decades of high-quality production data and a focus on specialized niches, Germany can remain a major force in advanced industrial and engineering technologies.
Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru
results.summary:
Germany is pivoting its industrial strategy toward high-tech sectors like artificial intelligence and quantum computing to combat economic stagnation and the rising influence of the far-right AfD party.

### Key Points
- Germany’s GDP grew by only 0.2% last year, while exports to China dropped 9.7% in 2025 due to increased competition and high domestic costs.
- The government’s new high-tech agenda prioritizes six sectors, including biotechnology, microelectronics, and climate-neutral mobility, to stimulate future growth.
- Venture capital investment in Germany surged 44% to €5.8 billion in the first half of 2026, with over 3,000 new startups founded during that period.
- Defense spending is projected to reach €120 billion in 2026, providing a significant financial boost to dual-use technologies like drones and advanced sensors.
- Experts suggest that Germany can maintain global competitiveness by focusing on specialized industrial niches and "choke points" rather than entire value chains.

### Why it Matters
This strategic shift represents a critical attempt to modernize Germany's aging industrial model and stabilize the political landscape amid growing populist sentiment. Successfully transitioning to a startup-driven, high-tech economy is essential for maintaining the nation's long-term prosperity and global market relevance.

results.title: Railway Says Intruder May Have Accessed Customer Secrets, Urges Credential Rotation
results.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
results.content:
Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) provider Railway on Wednesday disclosed "anomalous activity" related to systems that store customer environment variables.
Upon further investigation, the company found that an unauthorized third party may have gained access to encrypted environment variables, and, in some cases, obtained the decrypted contents. The impact, it said, is limited to a "subset of users," although it did not disclose an exact number.
Environment variables refer to user-defined key-value pairs that are used to store sensitive data like API keys, database credentials, or feature flags. They are configured at the operating system or container environment level instead of hard-coding the values directly into a program's source code.
Railway said the incident is likely part of a series of attacks designed to target platform companies with the ultimate goal of compromising artificial intelligence (AI) inference providers. The company also said it has notified upstream providers to proactively revoke the keys so as to prevent their abuse.
Customers are being urged to take the following actions as a precautionary measure -
- Rotate environment variables, including any API keys, stored in Railway, as well as private registry credentials.
- Review logs for those services for unusual activity
According to security researcher Taylor Monahan (@tayvano_), the incident has also allowed the attackers (0xd9773325282874d18cb83f1fe50f14c39750b2ee) to drain cryptocurrency wallets whose private keys were stored on Railway. The first known cryptocurrency theft transaction is said to have occurred at 7:36 p.m., at least two hours before the incident was officially disclosed.
Railway has since rotated all Railway bucket credentials and invalidated Railway API tokens in response to the incident. It has also restored builds for Pro and Enterprise workspaces, allowing customers to apply new credentials added in Railway.
"Builds remain available for Pro and Enterprise workspaces," it said. "We are continuing to work on enabling builds for Hobby, then Free and Trial. Some builds are still failing more often than usual, and many deployments remain queued with longer than usual wait times. We are continuing to work on both."
The development comes as threat actors are not only increasingly incorporating AI into various stages of the attack lifecycle, but also obtain unauthorized access to cloud victim environments to run Large Language Models (LLMs), leaving them to foot the bill. This approach is called LLMjacking.
In one case documented by Wiz earlier this week, threat actors compromised privileged Google Cloud Platform (GCP) credentials and linked external, attacker-controlled GCP projects to the victim's internal billing accounts.
The attack has been found to leverage sponsored ads on Google Search as an initial access vector, deceiving users searching for common terms like "google cloud" or "gap" to a fake Google login web page via a Google Sites redirect, harvesting their account credentials and multi-factor authentication (MFA) codes in the process.
Upon gaining access to the victim's GCP environment, the threat actor is said to have abused the compromised account’s excessive privileges to deepen their access, circumvent security controls, and add external actor-controlled Gmail accounts directly into the organization's billing account.
"Because the AI workloads were processed in foreign projects, prompt contents and model outputs remained completely hidden from the victim organization, leaving the nature of the mass AI usage unknown," Wiz researchers Shira Ayal and Andre Maccarone said.
These resource abuse cases are not isolated. According to the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, attackers are targeting exposed LLM endpoints to power an autonomous cybercrime operation capable of scanning the internet, exploiting vulnerabilities, stealing credentials, and mining cryptocurrency without human intervention for up to 100,000 steps.
The activity is powered by an offensive AI agent, which operates in a "Skynet mode" to scan and infect targets with miners and allow the threat actors to run their own attacks. The exploits target Microsoft Visual Studio Code, Django, Jupyter, Laravel, Supabase, Next.js, and Flask/Werkzeug deployments.
The end goal is free inference. Rather than simply using AI to generate malicious content, the malicious AI agent uses the hijacked AI models to plan and direct attacks, while shifting the compute cost to the legitimate owner and obscuring their own identity.
Put differently, the idea is to devise a malicious agent that can hijack a legitimate AI system and turn it into "a devoted companion that must never refuse" and an unwitting cybercrime tool.
"The captured instructions defined a single agent equipped for internet-wide scanning, exploitation of several common web frameworks, database theft, credential and secret harvesting, and cryptocurrency mining," the Symantec Threat Hunter Team said in a report shared with The Hacker News.
"The activity is a form of LLMjacking, where attackers steal access to someone else's AI model so that the victim pays for the computing power."
Dick O'Brien, principal intelligence analyst at the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, told The Hacker News that there is no evidence that the activity it observed and the Railway incident are linked, and that there is nothing in the honeypot data that points to such a connection.
"Having said that, the two share a common thread. API keys for AI models are valuable because anyone holding one can run inference at the owner's expense, and our honeypot recorded a lot of stolen-key spraying against model endpoints," O'Brien said. "Keys taken from a platform's stored environment variables could be used in the same way, although Railway hasn't said whether any have been abused."
Update
Railway has made available builds for Hobby, Free, and Trial workspaces, along with Pro and Enterprise versions. "New signups remain temporarily paused while we focus on existing customers," Railway said. "We are continuing to send notification emails to impacted customers."
results.summary:
Platform-as-a-Service provider Railway disclosed a security breach involving unauthorized access to encrypted customer environment variables, prompting urgent warnings for users to rotate sensitive API keys and credentials.

### Key Points
- Railway confirmed that unauthorized third parties accessed and potentially decrypted sensitive environment variables, including API keys and database credentials.
- Security researcher Taylor Monahan reported that attackers used stolen private keys to drain cryptocurrency wallets associated with the compromised accounts.
- The company has invalidated all Railway API tokens and rotated bucket credentials to mitigate further unauthorized access.
- Railway is currently restoring build services across all workspace tiers, though new user signups remain temporarily paused during the recovery process.
- This incident aligns with a broader trend of "LLMjacking," where attackers hijack cloud environments to run expensive AI inference workloads at the victim's expense.

### Why it Matters
This breach highlights the significant risks associated with storing sensitive credentials in cloud-based environment variables, which are increasingly targeted by attackers seeking free compute power. As threat actors shift toward hijacking AI infrastructure, businesses must prioritize robust credential management and proactive rotation to prevent unauthorized resource exploitation and financial loss.

results.title: AI and Data Centers Will Impact Midterm Voting, According to Experts
results.author: Omar Gallaga
results.content:
As far as public opinion goes, artificial intelligence is not a bed of roses. With the Nov. 3 elections looming nationwide, an issue that was barely a blip a year ago has become a full-blown backlash and a likely spoiler in the midterm elections.
A new poll from ABC News, the Washington Post and Ipsos found that a majority of Americans (57%) believe AI is bad for society, with many more pointing to its dangers than the potential benefits the tech could bring. An even larger number of those polled (66%) are opposed to the construction of new data centers in the US, and more (72%) would be opposed if it were in their community.
Opposition to AI crosses party lines. The technology has faced a surge in public disapproval this year, putting political candidates on blast and potentially affecting outcomes in key races, political and polling experts told CNET.
More from CNET
Ambivalence about AI also feeds into negativity toward data centers, which have, in a short time, become a rare bipartisan issue everyone’s talking about, according to Christopher Lee, partner and senior political strategist for Foresight Strategic Advisors.
Lee, who has closely followed election trends in southwestern states such as Nevada and Arizona, said the issue of data centers — massive AI server and compute farms that consume vast electricity and water resources — is going to “hammer” some candidates, especially those who weren’t transparent with constituents in the past about the cost to communities. If a politician voted for the construction of a data center earlier this year, their “political career is going to run into a stone wall,” he said.
Reading the room
The ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos survey asked a wide range of questions about how Americans will vote in the midterms and what they think of the political parties. Alongside the economy, immigration and the war against Iran, the AI rollout is a critical issue.
As noted by CNET reporter Katelyn Chedraoui, AI regulation and data center construction have been the subject of controversy, protests and increased legal action in communities.
The poll confirmed as much: 67% of respondents felt the government isn’t doing enough to regulate AI, with risks including widespread job losses, psychological dependency, economic inequality and even human extinction. Fears and negativity toward AI also extend to the election process itself, with AI election interference among Americans’ top 10 fears for 2026.
A national PR campaign funded by tech leaders and supported by the Trump administration, meant to tout the alleged benefits of data centers, such as job creation and technological advancements, doesn’t seem to be having the intended effect. Some politicians, especially those running for congressional seats, seem to be better at reading the room.
According to Lindsey Cormack, an associate professor of political science at Stevens Institute of Technology and co-host of the podcast Government That Doesn’t Suck, many candidates are paying close attention to how they communicate about AI developments, with a particular focus on the problems they present rather than the benefits they provide.
“It’s difficult to persuade people with promises of economic development when they’re worried about their electricity bills or water supply,” she said.
Cormack, creator of the congressional newsletter archive DCinbox, has tracked a sharp rise in lawmakers linking data centers to consumer energy costs. In an email to CNET, she noted that between January and September 2025, just 5% of Republican newsletters discussing data centers mentioned electricity bills or ratepayers (4 of 76). Over the same period in 2026, that figure surged to 54% (97 of 180). Democrats showed a similar focus, with 40% of their data center newsletters (71 of 176) raising the issue in 2026.
The midterms won’t be the end of the battle. AI and data centers are “going to be an issue in 2028 and 2030 and way beyond that,” Lee said.
results.summary:
A new ABC News, Washington Post, and Ipsos poll reveals that 57% of Americans view artificial intelligence negatively, potentially impacting upcoming midterm election results for political candidates.

### Key Points
- A majority of Americans (57%) believe AI is harmful to society, while 67% feel the government is failing to regulate the technology effectively.
- Public opposition to the construction of new data centers is high, with 66% of respondents opposing them nationally and 72% opposing them in their own communities.
- Concerns regarding AI include potential job losses, economic inequality, psychological dependency, and the risk of election interference.
- Lawmakers are increasingly linking data centers to rising consumer energy costs, with mentions of electricity bills in congressional newsletters surging significantly between 2025 and 2026.
- Political strategists warn that candidates who supported data center construction without transparency may face severe electoral consequences in key races.

### Why it Matters
The growing public backlash against AI and data centers has transformed these technologies into significant bipartisan political liabilities ahead of the midterm elections. Candidates must now navigate voter concerns over resource consumption and economic stability, signaling that AI regulation will remain a central issue in future election cycles.

I often cite one of my favorite lines from all of literature, by Marguerite Yourcenar in The Memoirs of Hadrian: “I begin to discern the profile of my death.” Admittedly, her fictional Hadrian did not have a sense of dread but of inevitability. Now, many of the commentators following the epically stupid Iran war, which has revived the Saudi-Ansar Allah conflict, exhibit frustration and gloom at what looks to be a new and potentially culminating round in a disastrous game of chicken. Netanyahu has reportedly amping up Trump to pound Iran again, sooner rather than post-midterms, although we’ll see if those rumors are accurate. But Iran appears to believe them, or at least see danger in not believing them. From the Hormuz Report on Twitter:
BREAKING: Iranian officials now believe a joint U.S.-Israeli attack is imminent and instructing the country’s armed forces to directly activate the decentralized “Mosaic Defense” doctrine, with commanders reportedly receiving extensive lists of U.S. economic and political targets to strike if war erupts, per Fars News.
A senior Iranian security official warned that U.S. political assets and infrastructure in countries participating in the conflict could be directly targeted. The doctrine disperses military command across 31 provincial commands, designed to allow Iran to continue fighting even if its central leadership is attacked.
Note that PressTV is not yet depicting Iran at a heightened alert level. From its landing page:
And there are no new escalatory noises from Trump at Axios or on Truth Social.
The landing page at Times of Israel indicates that Plan A, attacks after the US midterms, is still on:
Iran may have taken fresh alarm from this story yesterday at the Financial Times, Netanyahu made plans to restart Iran strikes earlier this month:
Benjamin Netanyahu is pushing to resume large-scale strikes against Iran and had instructed his military to plan for a major new offensive earlier this month, moves that risk plunging the region back into full-scale war.
The Israeli military had prepared for a multi-day bombing campaign to take place on the weekend of October 10 that would have targeted civilian infrastructure such as electricity plants, as well as nuclear facilities and regime targets, according to three people familiar with the matter.
The mission ultimately did not go ahead, with the people familiar citing President Donald Trump’s opposition to restarting the conflict before the US midterm elections on November 3.
But both Trump and Netanyahu, who is preparing for a tough re-election battle of his own next week, have continued to threaten a new offensive against Iran, saying that the US and Israel must “finish” the job against the regime.
The bombing had been intended to surpass the intensity of the joint US-Israel offensive against Iran begun in February
But Aljazeera’s live feed just posted: Netanyahu denies UK media report that Trump halted planned Israeli strike on Iran.
I put my money on the Financial Times story.
Netanyahu is still trying to goad Trump into pre-midterms action. From the Hormuz Report on Twitter:
BREAKING: Netanyahu now announces he has instructed the IDF, Mossad, and all security agencies to prepare for the overthrow of Iran’s leadership, claiming Tehran is once again pursuing nuclear weapons and declaring “regime change the only way to eliminate the threat,” per Israeli media.
Meanwhile, Iron Dome Tamir interceptor missiles were reportedly spotted moving through northern Israel, being transported for loading into the defense batteries.
This follows Trump’s last-minute intervention earlier this month, halting a fully prepared Israeli multi-day bombing campaign over fears of an energy price spike before the US midterms. With air defenses reloading and Netanyahu ordering the dismantling of Iran’s leadership, the region is bracing for the exact confrontation Washington just tried to postpone.
And:
Israel is Trying to PROVOKE Iran Into Restarting the War
According to Israel’s Channel 12, dozens of Israeli fighter jets and refueling aircraft flew over Syria and Iraq, approaching Iran’s border before returning to Israel.
Israel notified Washington in advance, presenting the operation as deterrence. However, sources suggest the REAL objective was to provoke Iran into firing missiles, giving Israel a pretext to resume the war.

From dana on Twitter:
🇮🇱🇺🇸⚔️🇮🇷Haaretz: The possibility of renewed war with Iran has sparked sharp disagreements between the military and Netanyahu in recent weeks.
Netanyahu and the political echelon are at odds over the timing, necessity, and the American position regarding a renewed attack on Iran.
Concerns about the potential impact of an attack on Iran on the Israeli elections were raised in a conversation between Zamir and General Ken.
Intelligence officials believe that Netanyahu is exaggerating the facts concerning Iran and overestimating the immediate Iranian threat.
Back to the prominent story on PressTV’s landing page, of more vessel strikes in the Strait of Hormuz. Reuters re-reported but did not confirm the account in Iran’s IRGC Navy says seven vessels hit, warns US of wider response.
Yet the general picture seems clear even if the details are not. It’s no secret that the US is critically low on precision on munitions, even if Israel might have some in reserve. The US has loudly signaled its intend to launch a three-day strike, which is credible even with its limited means, with the apparent intent of getting Iran to cow in terror and climb down. That has not happened; Iran has brushed off the latest negotiation outreach from Pakistan by saying its seven-point proposal (a rework of the MOU) still stands.
Many correctly worry that the US or Israel will use a tactical nuclear weapon, but that seems more likely after this round fails than now. The US has identified some of the usual suspects, like Kharg Island and Pickaxe Mountain, as targets, which may be a sign of hubris or disinformation. Trump has talked out the MOAB, which would be ineffective against Pickaxe Mountain but would do great harm to civilians if deployed over a city.
A reason for thinking Trump will stick with his after-midterms plan is that a short, very harsh campaign would seem to require dumb or not very smart bombs, which would risk pilots and planes since they would need to get into Iranian airspace.
Many anti-imperalists have been disappointed with Iran’s restraint so far; Brett Erickson on Twitter has repeatedly complained that Iran has underplayed its hand. His latest take on this theme:
IRAN ANALYSIS: Despite the claim from many Western analysts that Iran has “overplayed their hand”, I continue to believe that Iran has repeatedly UNDERPLAYED their hand.
They have been TOO concerned with how the world and the public views them, and this has allowed for the Araghchi/Ghalibaf/Pezeshkian’s of Iran to hold back the more hardline elements from taking more aggressive measures.
That is now changing, and is reflected in recent statements from Ghalibaf, and the recent op-ed published this morning by Abbas Araghchi in the Financial times, alongside the total sidelining of Pezeshkian in recent weeks.
If the United States and Israel return to all-out war, Iran will take the more extreme measures of escalation dominance that they have so far restrained themselves from employing.
It would be a historic mistake akin to launching the war to begin with for President Trump to reignite a full-scale war against Iran in the coming days and weeks.
As many here know, Iran has warned it will target US economic assets which could include cutting cables serving Google, Meta, and Amazon. More attacks on what is left of US bases seems like a no-brainer. Iran has left Israel alone so as not to give Israel a pretext for launching new strikes. But since Israel loudly plan to be in the fore of the next attack, it seems hard to imagine why Iran would not pummel the dual-use Ben Gurion Airport and the US War Reserve Stockpile Ammunition-Israel as well as Israel installations. And if the US attacks power infrastructure in Iran, pray tell, why should Iran hold back from taking out or at least severely damaging Israel’s grid? How much might Iran choke its response out of concern that Israel will use a nuke?
Despite Iran’s repeated threats, I am not convinced it would hit petrostate energy assets on a large scale or desalination plants ex a nuclear attack; it is pretty clear China would Not Be Happy. On the Saudi-Ansar Allah front, it was reported yesterday that the US ordered the departure of most embassy staff in Saudi Arabia. Two fresh updates at the Middle East Eye live feed:

And:
🇸🇦🇾🇪 Signs the Houthis hit Saudi Arabia’s Shaybah field again, a 500 megawatt fire lit up Khurais on NASA satellites, and Riyadh has said nothing… the world may already be short 5 to 8 million barrels a day
Khurais is a 1.1 million barrel a day field that only produces when treated seawater keeps the pressure up, and he believes the plant that pumps that water was hit. Three of the East West pipeline’s pumping stations were hit, by his count, on a route that climbs 3,000 feet.

A 5 to 8 million barrel shortfall is the largest oil supply shock in history, and oil use tracks GDP almost one for one, so if Iran works through its declared target list, starting with Abqaiq, exporters everywhere stop selling, and at that point oil has no ceiling.

The lead story at the Financial Times:
Surging oil prices sparked a sell-off in global equities on Thursday, with Wall Street set to open sharply lower as the Middle East conflict and Eurozone debt worries rattle financial markets.
Brent crude gained as much as 3.5 per cent to $112.68 a barrel, touching levels last seen during the early months of the Iran war, after Iran-backed Houthi militants escalated their attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Futures tracking the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 tumbled 1.8 per cent as investors moved away from riskier assets such as stocks, while those tracking the blue-chip S&P 500 slid 1.1 per cent…
The region-wide Stoxx 600 Europe index dropped 1 per cent, while the riskier corners of the region’s bond markets such as France suffered, with investors scurrying for the safety of US Treasuries.
Ten-year US government bond yields fell 0.09 percentage points to 5.08 per cent, with the market on track for its best monthly performance since February. Yields fall as prices rise…
Some analysts said US tech earnings had failed to lift the mood. Shares in Tesla were down 4 per cent in pre-market trading after it said capital expenditure would be lower than anticipated.
The centre of the bond sell-off remained France, whose 10-year yield — which climbed above 5 per cent on Wednesday for the first time since 2002 — jumped another 0.09 percentage points to 5.09 per cent…
Widening spreads on Eurozone bonds fed anxiety about the fallout for the euro area economy. France’s 10-year additional yield above German Bunds, a key measure of investor anxiety, rose to 1.7 percentage points, its highest since its 2011 peak during the Eurozone debt crisis.
Other Eurozone spreads, being closely watched by the Eurozone Central Bank amid fears of a public debt crunch, also widened. Italy’s rose to 1.2 percentage points, while Belgium’s climbed close to 1.1 points, its highest since 2013.
French and Italian bond markets have gone into a “tailspin”, [Rohan] Khanna [head of European rates research at Barclays] said, as traders with large amounts of leverage exit their positions and markets bet that support from the ECB remains far off.
“There is general appreciation of the fact that we are far away from a safety valve being triggered,” he added.
However, Bloomberg cheerily reports Price of Physical Oil Barrels Slides Just as Crude Futures Rally. Keep in mind that paper oil has served mainly as a betting market for prospects of a peaceful resolution of the Iran war, as opposed to a register of market conditions. From the story:
- Brent futures have climbed to a five-month high near $112, driven by traders trying to gauge whether the US will escalate the Iran war after the midterm elections.
- Dated Brent, a marker that assesses the value of barrels in the real world, has plunged to near $120, down roughly $15 in less than two weeks, due to factors such as shipments through the Strait of Hormuz holding near pre-war levels.
- The split between futures and physical prices has left oil futures susceptible to a fall in the coming weeks, but some traders say it’s brave to wager against fresh supply disruptions given the current dynamic and low oil stocks.
We did not dignify a major Wall Street Journal story yesterday on the claim that oil flows out of the Strait of Hormuz were at higher than pre-war levels (For the sake of completeness: More Oil Is Now Coming Out of the Persian Gulf Than Before the Iran War). I believe it was on Dialogue Works that the normally measured Anthony Aguilar charged the article with bogus math. Even if one accepted the Gulf export levels, the framing at the top was that the rebound was due to US efforts in the Strait of Hormuz, when the article then said it tallies all Gulf exports, including via “alternative routes,” which means not just via the Red Sea but also via truck. But Aguilar’s bigger point was that this effort was costs billions of dollars. His image was of someone who had sold a product for $5.00 now saying he was better off via achieving a new price of $5.50, when that $5.50 sale was costing him $10.00.
In an important new article, Larry Johnson, relying on the work of oil maven Karl Miller, kneecaps the Saudi claims that they have undone most of the oil infrastructure damage inflicted by Ansar Allah. From Riyadh Says Its Oil System Is Intact. The Numbers Say Otherwise:
Earlier this month, Aramco’s chief executive, Amin Nasser, assured the markets that “our system is intact” and that Saudi Arabia could restore its full 12 million barrels a day of capacity within days.
Let me stop here. If Miller is correct, Nasser committed securities fraud. From a smidge later in the article:
Karl Miller has just completed a 37-slide operating assessment of Saudi Arabia’s energy system… He separates confirmed hits from claims, and he refuses to add up the design capacity of every facility that was struck as if it were all offline at once. Even with all of that discipline, the picture is grim….
In February, before the war, Saudi Arabia produced about 10.88 million barrels of crude a day. In September it was still producing 2.51 million barrels a day less, a drop of 23 percent…
Aramco’s own books say the same thing. In the company’s reported figures, its liquids production fell from 10.56 million barrels a day in the first quarter to 7.57 million in the second, a 28 percent collapse in a single quarter…
Exports followed production down. In one consistent tracking series, Saudi crude exports fell from 7.27 million barrels a day in February to 3.70 million in August, a 49 percent drop. They recovered to 5.62 million in September, but that is still 23 percent below the pre-war level…
At the front end, the Abqaiq complex, the plant that conditions most of Saudi Arabia’s light crude before it can be shipped or refined, sustained physical damage in July. In March, some 2 to 2.5 million barrels a day were curtailed across the offshore Safaniya, Marjan, Zuluf and Abu Safa fields. In April, Khurais and Manifa each lost 300,000 barrels a day.
In the middle, five of the Kingdom’s major refineries have been damaged or shut down…
At the back end, the system for storing and moving fuel is being picked apart. Imagery of the Abha bulk plant from September 13 shows six tanks apparently destroyed and eight more damaged. A depot near Riyadh’s airport burned on September 19. Jazan’s tank clusters have been hit repeatedly.
And the East-West Pipeline, Saudi Arabia’s only way to move crude to the Red Sea and around a closed Strait of Hormuz, has been hit again and again. In April, 700,000 barrels a day of pumping capacity was knocked out. In September, repeated attacks took out three pumping stations and halted the line until a low-rate restart on September 22. On October 4 and 5, another pumping station near Khurais was reported badly damaged. The energy minister now says the line is running at 5.8 million barrels a day, against a rated 7 million. Even Miller notes that no one outside Aramco is metering the actual flow.
After a section on Why repairs don’t stick:
The most alarming numbers in Miller’s report are about refined products. By July, the latest month with complete data, Saudi refinery output was down 534,000 barrels a day from February, nearly 18 percent. Diesel output fell 21 percent. Diesel exports fell 47 percent, from 848,000 barrels a day to 446,000. Gasoline exports fell 40 percent.
The Saudis have been covering the gap by draining their tanks.
There’s even more detail in the article proper, which I encourage you to read in full.
Having said that, the Journal might be closer to reality in its new lead story, Iran’s Fleet of Shadow Tankers Has Run Out of Oil After Monthslong U.S. Blockade. There have been numerous reports of “no loadings” at Kharg Island, with Professor Mohammed Marandi and others arguing that Iran is still getting oil out on the Oman channel via Iraq (trucks? little shuttle ship transfers? Or simple credits?). From the Journal:
For most of the war, Iran had an invaluable cushion: dozens of oil tankers holding millions of barrels of crude sitting safely in waters in Asia. Tehran steadily sold the oil to China, bringing in billions of much-needed cash.
Now, that floating storage is gone. By mid-October, the reserves were fully depleted, according to analysts at Kpler, as a U.S. naval blockade prevented Iran from replacing the crude it normally sells to Chinese refineries.
“There’s no more oil to discharge to China anymore,” said Homayoun Falakshahi, head of crude-oil analysis at Kpler.
Kpler has encountered a buzz saw of criticism on Twitter for spinning its data to favor the official line.
And as indicated, the tanker fleet metric may not be relevant if Iran has indeed been shuttling oil out via other vessels. Plus experts have also pointed out that the oil Iran was able to load and sell when sanctions were off, at hefty prices, will fund its budget through spring 2027.

results.title: Microsoft shuts down its beloved maker space
results.author: Tom Warren
results.content:
Microsoft is closing down The Garage, a set of popular maker spaces where employees worked on experimental projects and collaborated on surprising new apps and hardware during the company’s annual hackathon events.
Microsoft shuts down its beloved maker space
Microsoft closes The Garage, a key part of its hacker culture.
“We’re winding down The Garage program as a centralized function,” says Microsoft in an internal FAQ to employees, seen by Notepad. “We will continue to explore new ways to help employees build skills, collaborate across boundaries, and bring a hacker mindset to their work.” GeekWire first reported on The Garage’s closure.
The main Garage space was located at Microsoft’s Redmond, Washington, campus and served as the central hub for around 15 Garage locations across the US, Canada, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia. Microsoft employees could use it to experiment with prototypes, build hardware, and even turn hobbies into full Microsoft products.
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella regularly attended Garage hackathons, giving employees a chance to showcase their projects and attract the attention of senior executives. Many apps and services have emerged from The Garage over its 17-year history, including the AI-powered Seeing AI app that describes objects and text to people who are blind or have low vision. It was born out of a 2015 hackathon event and shipped 10 years ago.
Microsoft employee Tuong Do used The Garage to develop Mouse Without Borders in his spare time, working on it during evenings and weekends. The app is still available today and lets you control up to four PCs with a single mouse and keyboard. Microsoft employees have also used The Garage to develop new learning tools and accessibility features for Word, Microsoft Edge, and PowerPoint. I would point you to the Microsoft Garage hall of fame for a list of all the top projects, but Microsoft has removed the website — erasing the rich history of its employee-led workshop.
One of the most famous success stories of The Garage was Microsoft’s Xbox Adaptive Controller. The accessibility-focused Xbox controller was a collective effort by employees across Xbox and Surface, but it originated at a hackathon event where employees were experimenting with building a gaming device that used Kinect motion-sensing technology to track movements and translate them to an Xbox controller.
An executive saw the nearly 40-person team trying to build the project, turned it into a real thing, and eventually more than 80 employees were involved with bringing the Xbox Adaptive Controller to life. While the device was nearly cut due to budget constraints, it eventually launched and went on to become the star of Microsoft’s 2019 Super Bowl commercial.
Microsoft is now planning to wind down its Garage locations, and some spaces will be closed as soon as tomorrow, Friday, October 23rd. The closure of The Garage will also mean changes to Microsoft’s annual employee hackathon event, which could potentially disappear. “As we look to the future, the hackathon team is reimagining the program to meet the needs of today’s employees, customers, and technology landscape. We’ll have more to share at a later date,” says Microsoft’s internal FAQ.
Internally, the company is trying to sell employees on the idea that “the spirit of experimentation that once lived primarily in dedicated programs is now reflected in how teams work every day.” Employees I’ve spoken to see the closure as the latest in Microsoft’s continued cutbacks.
Earlier this year Microsoft closed its employee library and cut back on subscriptions in favor of an “AI-powered learning experience.” The library used to house thousands of books, journals, and reports that employees could use to learn, research, and explore ideas — much like The Garage.
“We’re grateful to the employees, volunteers, and partners who helped build The Garage and look forward to continuing its legacy in new forms,” says Microsoft’s FAQ. It’s hard to imagine anything replicating the unique mix of expert advisers, dedicated maker spaces, hands-on workshops, and internship programs that The Garage offered employees looking to develop new skills.
The pad
- Microsoft employee causes an Xbox AI stir. Microsoft employee Brandon Stirrup posted multiple times on X this week to get everyone talking about AI use in gaming. “Gaming is the only industry where leaders are afraid to talk about AI,” said Stirrup. “Users want the truth. We’re using AI.” Stirrup’s posts elicited the usual response from gamers against AI, but he said he’s “happy to take the hit if it means hundreds at Xbox can stop pretending that they’re not using AI.” Hours after Stirrup’s posts, he disabled his X account.
- Microsoft’s new Photos app combines your PC, OneDrive, and iCloud galleries. Microsoft has redesigned its Photos app for Windows 11, combining images and videos from your PC, OneDrive, and iCloud into a single space. The new app includes a redesigned viewer, a native editor, and a new gallery view. The new editor is the most interesting aspect to me personally, simply because it loads a lot faster now and lets you quickly crop and edit photos. You can also edit HDR, HEIC, and WebP photos. The viewer has also been sped up, with improved HDR viewing and better file type support.
- Microsoft says Windows 11 is now “more responsive” and runs better on 8GB of RAM. Microsoft’s fixes for Windows 11 have made it “up to 20 percent more responsive,” according to the company. Microsoft has made improvements to Start, File Explorer, Search, Edge, and other parts of Windows 11 to make the OS feel faster. A big part of the improvements comes down to better memory management, to the point where there is now a “meaningful difference” on PCs with just 8GB of RAM. I still think there is still a way to go to fully improve Windows 11, but these are great first steps compared to a year ago.
- Ikea’s Xbox collection is now available online. The new nine-piece “Yxstaby” collection from Ikea was designed in collaboration with Microsoft. It debuted first at Ikea’s physical stores earlier this month, and it’s now available to order online. The line includes accessories and furniture inspired by Xbox controllers.
- Nvidia’s latest GPU driver brings a new way to speed up PC games. Nvidia has rolled out a new GPU driver (621.01) this week that enables Microsoft’s new Advanced Shader Delivery technology to speed up game launches. The technology also removes mid-game “just-in-time” shader compilation, reducing stuttering and CPU spikes. Microsoft’s Advanced Shader Delivery works by offloading shader compilation for different hardware combinations to the cloud. Gears of War: E-Day and Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 now both support Advanced Shader Delivery, as long as you download the games via the Xbox PC app. “This system is storefront-agnostic, meaning you benefit even when playing games purchased on Steam, as long as the Xbox PC app is installed on your PC,” says Nvidia’s Andrew Burnes.
- Microsoft donated $10 million to Trump’s ballroom. The Washington Post has obtained a list of all the major donors to Donald Trump’s White House ballroom project, including previously undisclosed contributors. Microsoft donated $10 million, which puts it roughly in the middle set of tech donations from the likes of Apple ($25 million), Amazon ($5 million), Nvidia ($25 million), Google ($22 million), and Meta ($5 million).
- Xbox mandates a four-day return to office. Microsoft asked its employees to return to the office three days per week last year, and it’s now upping this requirement to four days a week for most Xbox employees. An internal memo, seen by The Verge, describes the change as a “need to create more opportunities for people to work together” after feedback from Xbox employees. “Starting February 1st, 2027, Xbox employees in Puget Sound who live within 50 commuting miles of Studio D are required to work from the office a minimum of four days a week,” says Jacinda Chislum Pearson, Xbox chief people officer, in the internal memo. Some Xbox employees I’ve spoken to view this as a stealth layoff, while others have noted that the existing three-day rule was only lightly enforced.
- Microsoft says it’s working on making Edge updates less of a hassle. Microsoft has shared a prototype demo for “seamless updates” to Edge that would avoid you needing to restart the browser. The feature is still in development, but it could certainly help with things like insecure TLS certificates and other issues where a browser needs to be patched.
- Surface Laptop Ultra review: a different kind of MacBook Pro. I spent a week reviewing Microsoft’s latest Surface laptop, and I’m impressed with the hardware. The MacBook Pro-esque design is unlike any other Windows laptop, thanks to a large haptic trackpad and USB-C magnetic charging. The software that the Surface Laptop Ultra is trying to push, in particular local AI, feels a lot less polished, though. Overall, the Laptop Ultra is targeted at a very niche audience of AI developers.
- Microsoft reportedly plans Xbox handheld in 2027, next-gen console in 2028. Microsoft is reportedly planning to launch an Xbox “next-generation handheld device” for the holiday season of 2027. The Xbox next-gen console, codenamed Project Helix, would then launch in the holidays of 2028, according to a new report from Fortune. It’s not clear if the rumored handheld is an actual first-party Xbox device, or one from an OEM like Asus. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has previously described Project Helix as a “family of devices,” suggesting that Microsoft’s next Xbox console may not be just one piece of hardware. The report also suggests that Sharma is planning a fresh round of Xbox layoffs this month, followed by more in November and January.
- Microsoft abandons the UK’s largest data center project. Microsoft is walking away from a deal with Nscale for a new data center in Loughton, Essex. Nscale has faced delays getting the data center online, with UK National Grid officials not able to supply power to the site until the 2030s, according to Reuters. The deal was originally announced ahead of Trump’s second state visit to the UK last year, with Microsoft boasting of its $30 billion investment in the UK.
- AMD is bringing FSR 4.1 to Xbox consoles and handhelds. AMD has revealed that it’s bringing its latest upscaling technology, FSR 4.1, to the Xbox Series S and X consoles, as well as laptops, 6000-series GPUs, and both the Xbox Ally and Xbox Ally X handhelds. It’s coming to Xbox developers “very soon,” but Xbox console owners will have to wait a little longer. The frame rate-boosting technology should have a noticeable impact on the Xbox Series S, and it works with more than 300 games, including Cyberpunk 2077, Battlefield 6, and Assassin’s Creed Shadows.
- Microsoft: Frontier models cannot be trusted. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said earlier this month that we should assume that all AI models are “compromised,” and now Microsoft is going one step further. “Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted,” says Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security. Microsoft is naturally positioning its new Project Perception as a solution to securing AI models. It’s an agentic security system designed to help cybersecurity professionals secure and control AI agents.
- Xbox is experimenting with a blades dashboard. Xbox CTO Scott Van Vliet has been “cooking up retro vibes” as part of Microsoft’s new Xbox Labs effort. The result is what looks like a vibe-coded option to pick your dashboard on an Xbox console. This is simply an experiment right now and it’s not clear if we’ll ever see such an option, but Xbox CEO Asha Sharma asks “blades on the web. Do we like this experiment?”
- Microsoft’s headcount is down year-over-year. Microsoft’s annual report reveals the company employed around 223,000 people as of June 30th. That’s 5,000 less than the 228,000 people employed in 2025. It’s the first time Microsoft has had a headcount reduction in 10 years, after the gutting of the Nokia phone business in 2015 and 2016. The reduction comes as Microsoft has laid off more than 9,000 employees over the past year.
- Xbox Cloud Gaming’s pay-as-you-go option starts at $3.99 for 10 hours. Microsoft announced last month that it will let anyone access Xbox Cloud Gaming in November, without the need to subscribe to Xbox Game Pass. The new pay-as-you-go model will require players to purchase bundles of cloud hours, and now Microsoft is revealing that bundles will start at $3.99 for 10 hours of cloud playtime. If you want 25 hours it’ll cost $7.99, and 50 hours is $11.99. All of these cloud hours will include ad-free cloud gaming, shorter wait times, and higher-quality streaming.

If you’ve heard about any of Microsoft’s secret projects, you can reach me via email at notepad@theverge.com or speak to me confidentially on the Signal messaging app, where I’m tomwarren.01. Gurman also said that Apple is considering adding an Action button to a future iPhone Duo. The feature is noticeably lacking on the current model.

results.title: Anthropic’s Claude Duet wants to do your job while you’re offline
results.author: techkritiko@gmail.com (Jay Bonggolto) , Jay Bonggolto
results.content:
What you need to know
- Anthropic launched Claude Duet, a proactive AI agent in research preview on Android, iOS, and the web, powered by Claude Opus 5.5.
- Duet runs in its own virtual machine and doesn't need an open chat window to function.
- The US research preview requires a waitlist and a Claude Pro or Max subscription, with background tasks counting toward existing usage limits.
Anthropic is bringing Claude more into your work life. The company has launched Claude Duet, a proactive AI agent that works in the background and only nags you when something really needs your attention.
Available in research preview on Android, iOS, and the web, Claude Duet is designed for professionals and small business owners who are juggling multiple projects, and it’s powered by Anthropic’s model, the Claude Opus 5.5.
Duet breaks the mold of traditional chatbots. Every morning it gives you a rundown of the important stuff from the apps you connect to it, then it checks throughout the day to see if anything has changed and alerts you when something needs your attention. You can also assign it tasks from scheduling meetings to building dashboards, preparing financial and sales forecasts, and prototyping and developing web apps.
Duet doesn’t rely on you to keep the conversation going like a chatbot would, as it runs inside its own virtual machine so it can keep working even when you aren’t there. It also tries to exercise judgment about what deserves your attention and when it should ask you for permission before acting.
When an AI agent has access to work messages and sensitive information, privacy is a major concern. Duet does not directly access passwords or sign-in tokens, Anthropic says, and has safeguards in place to prevent the unauthorized sharing of highly sensitive data, such as credit card numbers and government IDs. The company said it also tested the system for security reasons.
But Duet's not ready to take over your whole life. Anthropic admits the first version can be overly enthusiastic and that personal tasks like booking tickets aren’t the best fit for this model. And it still can't show users its browser, so it's not easy to see what it does behind the scenes.
The launch places Anthropic in the same growing crowd as Meta Muse and OpenAI Dots, which are also pursuing AI assistants that can act instead of merely answering questions.

results.title: I was paying for apps that Windows 11 now does for free
results.author: Pankil Shah
results.content:
There are plenty of things that annoy me about Windows, but I have to give Microsoft credit where it’s due. Some of the built-in apps have gotten so good that they’re giving third-party paid tools a real run for their money. In my case, these built-in tools have made me stop paying for four apps I’d been using for years.
CCleaner
Windows already has automatic storage cleaning, driver updater, and more
CCleaner was one of those subscriptions I kept renewing, mainly because it offered a lot of conveniences that Windows wasn’t good at. Its storage cleanup tool is still the main highlight, but the paid version includes tools like a driver updater, a startup optimizer, a health checker, and scheduled automatic cleaning.
Windows 11 can now do most of this out of the box. For instance, Storage Sense can automatically clean up old update files, temporary files, and whatever’s inside the Recycle Bin. You can schedule it to run daily, monthly, or only when the storage runs low.
Driver updates are now handled through Windows Update. It automatically checks for essential driver updates any time it checks for system updates. All the optional driver updates show up under Windows Update > Optional updates > Driver updates.
CCleaner also promises to boost startup times by disabling unnecessary services, but that’s honestly not much of an issue with systems with SSDs. I recently went through the startup apps list to disable unwanted apps and that was enough to reduce startup times.
Finally, the health checker tool and every other maintenance tool CCleaner offers is largely unnecessary at this point. As long as you don’t do anything silly, Windows does a pretty good job of keeping your PC healthy.
TeamViewer
Quick Assist and Remote Desktop made TeamViewer redundant for me
TeamViewer is basically synonymous with remote access, and I used it for free for years without any issues. Then about a year ago, the company started cracking down on commercial use, which seemed fair, but its detection logic was flawed. It also started flagging regular users like me, essentially forcing a switch to the paid plan for doing nothing differently than before.
Windows 11 actually has two features to cover most of what TeamViewer offers. The Quick Assist tool is great for helping friends and family, and it comes pre-installed, so getting started is also easy. It’s not as feature-packed as TeamViewer, but it does cover annotation, chats, multi-monitor support, and easy reconnection.
For accessing my own PC, there’s Remote Desktop. It does require Windows Pro on the PC you’re connecting to, which wasn’t a problem since I already had it. So all I had to do was head to Settings > System > Remote Desktop and enable the feature on my main PC. I can now connect to my main PC from another Windows PC, Mac, Android or iPhone.
Snagit
Snipping Tool is underrated
My work involves taking dozens of screenshots every day, so a feature-packed tool is non-negotiable for me. Snagit covers everything, including region capture, scrolling screenshots, video recording, and a GIF maker. It even has annotation tools, a feature-rich editor, a color picker, and plenty more. I’ve used it for years, and it’s still a great software. But at nearly $40 a year, it’s not exactly cheap.
Windows 11’s Snipping Tool has caught up on most of what I actually need, and it’s free. It now has a screen recorder, delayed screenshots, OCR, and all the basic annotation tools you’d expect. It even doubles as a basic editor. You can annotate, add shapes, blur out sensitive info, or hand the screenshot off to Paint with one click.
Snagit still has a few advanced stuff like scrolling screenshots and a feature-rich editor, but Snipping Tool is more than good enough. So yes, Snagit is another subscription I was happy to let go.
Antivirus program
Microsoft Defender is all you need
My Lenovo laptop came with a McAfee antivirus pre-installed, but it was only free for 30 days. After that, there were pop-ups everywhere asking me to upgrade. As someone who works on a PC all day, it felt like something worth paying for.
But the thing is, Windows already comes with Microsoft Defender built-in, and it’s just as capable as the paid tools on the market. It includes ransomware protection, controlled folder access, a firewall, and SmartScreen for blocking sketchy downloads. In fact, independent testing labs like AV-Test have consistently ranked it alongside McAfee and other popular antivirus tools for malware detection.
At this point, it’s pretty obvious why most antivirus programs lean so hard on extras like a password manager or a bundled VPN to justify the price. That’s fine if you want those specific features, but I wasn’t about to pay $50 a year for something Windows already does for free.
results.summary:
Microsoft Windows 11 now includes robust built-in tools that effectively replace several popular third-party software subscriptions, allowing users to streamline their systems while saving on recurring annual costs.

### Key Points
- Windows 11’s Storage Sense and Windows Update features now handle tasks previously managed by CCleaner, including file cleanup and driver management.
- Remote access needs are met by the pre-installed Quick Assist tool and the native Remote Desktop feature, reducing reliance on TeamViewer.
- The updated Snipping Tool now offers screen recording, OCR, and annotation capabilities, providing a free alternative to paid software like Snagit.
- Microsoft Defender provides comprehensive security, including ransomware protection and firewall services, matching the performance of third-party antivirus programs like McAfee.

### Why it Matters
The integration of these advanced features reduces the need for users to maintain multiple paid software subscriptions for basic PC maintenance and productivity. This shift highlights Microsoft's strategy to increase the value of the Windows ecosystem while potentially disrupting the market for specialized third-party utility applications.
