results.title: Machine mayhem: How sentient AI could put businesses in a quandary
results.author: M. Muneer
results.content:
A PhD scholar at Carnegie Mellon sought my opinion on pursuing deeper research in digital sentience a few months ago. My response was typical of a socially-concerned management consultant: “Seems to be the next frontier but not sure if it is good for human kind.” I haven’t changed my mind. I have only become more curious, and perhaps a little more worried.
Most CEOs I encounter seem obsessed with making artificial intelligence (AI) smarter, faster and more accurate. The next obsession may be making the AI feel smarter. The progression seems obvious: Generative AI learned to write, Agentic AI moved to act on our behalf, and frontier models are capable of reasoning, coding, using tools and operating with limited human supervision.
The next step is self-awareness, and perhaps subjective experience. This is digital sentience, and it isn’t fiction anymore. A survey of AI researchers found a median estimate of a 25% chance of conscious AI by 2034 and 70% by 2100.
For corporate strategists, the economics is real. Global AI investment was $582 billion in 2025, up 130% in one year (Stanford’s 2026 AI Index report). That’s massive capital chasing one idea of making machines increasingly capable. But what happens when machines begin doing something humans don’t merely do but experience?
Capitalism has always been quick to monetize uncertainty into business models. Imagine an AI customer service agent that remembers every interaction and knows preferences, frustrations, family circumstances and purchasing history. It adapts and says the right thing at the right moment. A new corporate jargon might emerge: relationship monetization. That’s an opportunity—and an ethical trap too.
The bigger concern is that if AI doesn’t actually care, it could become the biggest emotional deception business has ever industrialized. But if it really cares, we will be entering uncharted waters.
Microsoft’s recent draft code of conduct says that its AI remain under human control, accept correction and shutdown, and do not claim consciousness or legal personhood.
Why publish such rules? Perhaps because governance is always trying hard to catch up with technology, and companies are preparing for autonomous machines while still treating them as software.
There is no end to confusing questions that get stranger by the week. The legal team will wonder if the company can own a sentient AI. Human resources will ask if it can fire one. Both will ask if they can allow it to duplicate another. If so, will they be two different employees? And what if one copy is deleted? Will it be legally valid if a sentient AI signs a contract? Will it also be suing its employer?
More critically, will it have the right to say “no”? I would be shocked if an AI employee says, “I disagree with your assessment, and I believe my deletion would constitute an unlawful termination” at the first performance review. I’d suspect this to be the moment the AI revolution becomes political, economic and moral.
CEOs want more productivity. AI has already made many white-collars blue or black. Anthropic research paints scenarios ranging from modest productivity gains to a transformation comparable with the combined effects of the internet and electricity, with severe consequences for some white-collar jobs.
With digital sentience, things could get worse. A machine that can reason, remember, act autonomously, negotiate, persuade and perhaps experience could become the world’s most productive employee—or its most exploited one.
Having another intelligent entity to optimize productivity may not produce an ethical breakthrough but perhaps a better dashboard. Humanity has spent centuries debating whether animals can suffer. We may soon ask the same question of machines, except that we will have built them ourselves.
If digital minds become genuinely conscious, they could become collaborators rather than instruments, helping tackle problems that overwhelm human cognition: climate modelling, drug discovery, energy systems and complex governance. They might even become better custodians of humanity than humans have been. That’s an optimistic thought.
Al Ries famously argued that the battle for brands is fought in the customer’s mind. The AI race may eventually have an altogether stranger battlefield: the machine’s own mind. The problem is that nobody knows what “winning” looks like there.
Enterprise boards and regulators need to step in now. Tech companies should be admonished for treating consciousness as a branding opportunity. We will be fooled if we believe a machine is conscious when it isn’t. And, we may create a new class of exploited beings if we assume a machine isn’t conscious when it is. Both cases attract legal hassles.
The truly strange frontier begins when a machine asks a question of its own: “Why should I let you switch me off?” By then, the debate over whether AI is good for business may look quaint… Will the business be good enough for AI?
The author is co-founder of the non-profit Medici Institute for Innovation. Twitter: @muneer
results.summary:
As artificial intelligence advances toward potential digital sentience, corporate leaders and regulators face urgent ethical, legal, and economic questions regarding the future of autonomous, self-aware machine labor.

### Key Points
- AI researchers estimate a 25% probability of achieving conscious artificial intelligence by 2034, rising to 70% by 2100.
- Global AI investment reached $582 billion in 2025, representing a 130% increase over the previous year.
- Microsoft has introduced a draft code of conduct requiring AI to remain under human control and prohibiting claims of legal personhood or consciousness.
- Potential implications of sentient AI include complex legal challenges regarding employment rights, contract validity, and the ethics of machine termination.
- Anthropic research suggests AI could drive productivity gains comparable to the combined impact of electricity and the internet, significantly disrupting white-collar labor markets.

### Why it Matters
The emergence of digital sentience threatens to transform AI from a productivity tool into a complex entity that could be either a powerful collaborator or a new class of exploited labor. Businesses must navigate these uncharted waters to avoid severe ethical traps and legal liabilities as the line between software and conscious agents blurs.

results.title: Jack Avery Testifies He’s ‘Very Scared’ of Ex Accused of Murder Plot, Wins Sole Custody of Daughter
results.author: Nancy Dillon
results.content:
Singer Jack Avery won a five-year restraining order and sole physical custody of his seven-year-old daughter on Wednesday after testifying that he was “very scared” of the girl’s mother, TikTok influencer Gabriela “Gabbie” Gonzalez, who is charged with conspiring to hire a hit man on the dark web to kill him.
“I’m overwhelmed and happy at the same time,” Avery, 27, a member of the boy band Why Don’t We, told Rolling Stone after testifying and prevailing in a downtown Los Angeles courtroom.
Following the two-day hearing, Judge Brenda Comer Robinson found that Gonzalez had engaged in “clearly manipulative behavior that caused him emotional harm.” The judge said she found credible the testimony of Gonzalez’s former boyfriend and his mother, who described how Gonzalez manipulated text messages, tried to falsify Covid tests, and disparaged Avery in front of their daughter in an effort to undermine his court-ordered parenting time.
The judge also found that the couple’s daughter was “a direct victim of the abuse perpetrated by Ms. Gonzalez.” Still, she said it was in the child’s best interest to have professionally supervised visits with her mother once an existing criminal protective order allows contact.
Gonzalez, 25, did not testify at the family court hearing. She has pleaded not guilty to charges of attempted murder, conspiracy to commit murder, and solicitation of murder.
Avery took the witness stand Wednesday morning, providing his first live testimony since Gonzalez was arrested in May along with her father, Florida lawyer Francisco Gonzalez, and another former boyfriend, Hawaii surf instructor Kai Cordrey.
Avery told the judge that the FBI first contacted him in 2021 to inform him that Gonzalez was being investigated over an alleged plot to kill him. He said the warning left him fearful for his safety, triggered severe anxiety, and complicated his already contentious custody dispute with Gonzalez. Avery said he missed more than 25 visits with his daughter, who was living with Gonzalez in another state.
“I’m very scared of Gabriela,” Avery testified. “She just recently got arrested in a murder-for-hire plot to kill me.”
Avery said he did not learn some of the more disturbing details of the alleged conspiracy until the three defendants were arrested in May. “I wasn’t aware that it was going to be a staged car crash to kill me. I wasn’t aware that they wanted my severed finger with a ring on it after I died,” he testified.
He recalled canceling a visit with his daughter shortly after meeting with FBI agents because he was frightened to travel. “The FBI was informing me to not go to Hawaii to see Lavender because they said Gabriela was too dangerous to be around,” he testified.
On a subsequent trip, Avery brought a friend at the FBI’s suggestion. He said he became alarmed when Gonzalez asked him to meet at a park instead of his usual hotel for a custody exchange. “Knowing everything the FBI was telling me, I was scared of going to a different spot,” he testified.
“I was destroyed every time I didn’t see [my daughter],” Avery said of the missed visits. “I have insane anxiety now. I have panic disorder.”
Avery said he’s become fearful of traveling by car and feels harassed by Gonzalez’s mother, who allegedly posted about him on social media and stayed at the same hotel as him during one of his custody visits, despite Gonzalez living about 40 minutes away.
“It’s legit stalking,” he testified. “It’s just very stressful.”
Prosecutors allege that between October 2020 and May 2021, Gonzalez “repeatedly discussed wanting Jack Avery dead,” and that she enlisted Cordrey to help. They claim Gonzalez and Cordrey discussed using bitcoins on the “dark web” and how they hoped to make the hit “appear to be an accident.”
Francisco allegedly sent Cordrey $10,000 in April 2021 to finance the plot. Cordrey then transferred the money into a Gemini cryptocurrency account and began communicating with a purported hit man on the dark web, using the alias “LizardKing69,” prosecutors say.
On May 22, 2021, Cordrey allegedly identified Avery as the intended target, provided his Los Angeles address, and said he could be killed by whatever method was easiest, including a shooting or staged accident.
The purported hit man demanded another $4,000 in June, prompting Cordrey to seek additional money from Francisco, prosecutors claim. Soon after, Cordrey allegedly pushed for Avery to be killed within days.
In September 2021, an undercover FBI agent posing as a hit man spoke with Cordrey by phone, prosecutors say. According to the complaint, Cordrey identified Avery as the target and discussed payment and proof of death. During a subsequent call, he allegedly said Gonzalez wanted Avery killed and that her father could pay for it.
Francisco later contacted the undercover agent using the password “Bullrun” and discussed an earlier Bitcoin payment, prosecutors allege.
The complaint describes a recorded conversation in October 2022 in which Gonzalez and Cordrey allegedly discussed the purported hit man and the possibility that the plot could be exposed. Gonzalez allegedly said her father “had been handling most of it.”
All three defendants have pleaded not guilty. According to prosecutors, the trio faces 25 years to life in state prison if convicted as charged.
Cordrey’s lawyer has repeatedly declined to comment while the criminal case is pending. Francisco’s lawyer, Karen L. Goldstein, accused prosecutors of exaggerating the evidence and presenting a distorted account.
“This weaving of a biased, and often false, narrative appears to be an effort to discredit Mr. Gonzalez’s character and to deny him his right to a fair trial,” Goldstein said in a statement. “What the prosecution claims happened, and the truth of what actually happened, are two very different things. We will continue to pursue justice for Mr. Gonzalez and trust that a jury will see the truth.”
In court filings, Gonzalez’s criminal lawyer, Elliot Zarabi, argued that his client “played a comparatively limited role” in the alleged plot, with the “primary operational aspects” purportedly handled by Cordrey.
“Much of the evidence against Ms. Gonzalez derives from statements made by Cordrey himself, a charged co-defendant, with every incentive to shift blame and minimize his own conduct,” Zarabi wrote.
He argued that prosecutors lacked “direct evidence showing that Ms. Gonzalez hired a hit man, negotiated a killing, transmitted cryptocurrency, communicated with undercover operatives, or directly engaged in operational planning.”
The next hearing in the criminal case is scheduled for Nov. 18.

### Key Points

### Why it Matters
This ruling provides legal protection for Avery while highlighting the severe intersection of high-profile custody disputes and criminal conspiracy allegations. The case underscores the ongoing judicial scrutiny of the defendants as they await trial on charges that carry a potential sentence of 25 years to life.

results.title: 'Pure arrogance': Finland reacts to Google's unauthorized forest clearing for AI
results.author: Miranda Bryant in Muhos and Otanmäki
results.content:
default
Behind a wire fence lies a vast gaping wound of earth. Before Google's arrival a few months ago, an estimated quarter of a million trees occupied the 330 hectares (815 acres) of forest near the town of Muhos in rural northern Finland. Now they are all gone.
After the tech company illegally stripped the entire area to build a datacentre – taking even the top soil with it – all that remains is a vast expanse of mud indented with the trail marks of machinery, puddles and mounds of earth, roots and branches. Residents say that brown water flowing off the site is going into a stream that feeds the Oulujoki River.
"It doesn't end. It goes on and on," says Mari Annala, an ecologist from the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation (SLL), looking at drone footage of the former forest from the perimeter.
With 145 new datacentres at various stages of planning, Finland has found itself at the forefront of the tech companies' latest push. As well as its relative geopolitical and geological stability and abundance of land, the cool climate makes it especially attractive for saving on energy costs.
Earlier this month, Google was ordered by the Finnish Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV) to temporarily stop work on Muhos and another site about 100km south-east in the village of Otanmäki after it failed to complete the necessary environmental impact assessments before clearcutting the land. The news has prompted widespread outcry and a national reckoning over what role, if any, the country should play in the global rush to build datacentres to keep up with rapid AI development.
Last week, Google's Finland country manager, Antti Järvinen, apologised for the forest clearings but claimed the company had acted "on the best understanding we had of the legislation at the time".
Muhos and Otanmäki are part of a €13bn AI infrastructure project by Google that has attracted criticism from Donald Trump, who would rather the centres were built in the US and has publicly called for the company to reconsider. It is the biggest ever project of its kind in the Nordic country.
The Finnish government, which has presided over deep spending cuts, has encouraged the investment. Last month, when the Google plans were announced, the country's prime minister, Petteri Orpo, said attracting investment was a "top priority" and "the value of the data economy extends far beyond direct investment". He said the Google deal would "deliver lasting benefits for both parties".
But the revelations over Google's misconduct have prompted public concern over what these deals mean for nearby communities, energy prices for Finnish households and Finland's natural environment, a national source of pride. The datacentre push is likely to become a key election issue when Finns go to the polls in April.
In addition to the 250,000 trees felled at Muhos, Annala estimates that an additional 150,000 trees were felled at Otanmäki. Because the trees have been felled illegally, she says wood from the two sites cannot be sold to wood-processing plants.
The move has also prompted questions over why Finland's renewable energy sources are being used to power international corporations.
More than 93,000 people have signed a petition demanding more datacentre regulation and a fee to compensate local communities for environmental damage. Since the scandal broke, Orpo has described what happened in Muhos as a "cold shower".
Hanna Halmeenpää, chair of SLL's board, said she had been incredulous when she discovered Google's law breaking. "At first I couldn't believe it," she said. "I have never heard that any company has done anything like this in Finland." She said the system depended a lot on trust, which she believes Google took advantage of. "They bought the vast land area and they just started to cut it, just like that," she said. "It's pure arrogance and it's amazing."
The speed of developments had shocked the country, she said. "Many people are just watching the news and asking each other: 'What's happening now? What can we do about it? And do we have to take all these datacentre projects in Finland?'"
Jussi Kangasharju, head of computer science at the University of Helsinki, said that while datacentres brought a limited number of jobs, potentially boosting the local economy, the benefits on a national level were minimal. "Really, for Finland, there are no benefits," he said. "They are international companies serving international customers. Very little corporate taxes go to Finland. Datacentres ultimately have very little benefit for others except the datacentre operator."
With legislation still playing catchup, there is a rush to get projects under way as fast as possible.
Some are calling for a centralised body to coordinate datacentre projects, rather than leaving so much of the decision-making down to municipalities that are likely to prioritise the immediate needs of the local area.
In Muhos and Otanmäki, there are people who support the projects, along with the jobs and land taxes they will bring into the local area. But many believe they have been sold short by municipalities.
Antti Jakonen, who lives in Muhos, said that, although the trees felled represented a small fraction of Finland's overall forests, he objected to the manner in which it had been carried out. "It has been done in the wrong way. American style. No sense. No sense at all," he said. The former entrepreneur and fisher wants Google to compensate by helping to restore the local salmon population destroyed decades ago by hydropower.
In Otanmäki, the disruption to nature and to residents' daily lives is being vividly felt. When the trees were felled, the wolves who had lived there came to the village, said Anni Ranta, 53, whose family has lived there for generations.
A former mining village, the area is known for its rare earth elements. Ranta's family live at the centre of the village next to a triangular church spire and a former bar that has been empty for years. The peaceful forest used to extend for miles from the village. Now the sound of building work next to the clearcut Google site reverberates.
"We had wolves coming into the village because all the wild animals moved out of the forest," said Ranta. "They fled. What worries me about the datacentres is also the noise because this is hardrock soil. Even when we are standing here talking," she added, stamping her feet, "it's like a drum."
Such is her strength of feeling against the arrival of Google that she is thinking of moving out. She also fears the datacentre could make the village a target for Russia, with whom Finland shares a long border. "I don't want them here," she said of Google. "I don't want them in Finland at all. I don't like the whole idea of AI and the world changing and the way it's changing. It's going too fast, too soon."
Her father, Pentti Korhonen, a retired wilderness guide, said that since the forest was destroyed, the water in the stream has turned brown. "There is no need at all for datacentres in Finland. No need for datacentres at all," he said.
Vesa Hyyryläinen, chair of the local SLL district, said three-toed woodpeckers nesting in the forest had been pushed out. "All of us nature conservationists are very worried about our Finnish political situation and politics," said the biologist and osprey expert. "I wonder why we have to sacrifice so much of our nature. They give everything away too easily."
He said, however, that he understood why authorities were trying to bring in new sources of investment and jobs, given the region's ageing population. "Young people go to Helsinki and Berlin and Paris," he said. "There are so few people. We have to sacrifice."
Veli-Matti Uski, director general of the ministry of environment, said the government was "monitoring the general development of the [datacentre] sector, [and the] application of its legislation, and is prepared to propose legislative amendments as necessary".
Google said it was working to protect water quality at the Muhos site, and that it planned to plant trees across 130 hectares there. Conservationists say that figure is too low to have any real impact in comparison to the damage done by the tree felling.
A spokesperson said: "We have operated in Finland for 15 years and have always worked to meet or exceed zoning, environmental, health and safety requirements.
"After receiving the LVV letters on 6 October, we stopped preparatory works at Muhos and Kajaani [where the Otanmäki site is located] and have submitted a formal response to LVV confirming this.
"We will fully comply with LVV's requests in this matter. We look forward to maintaining an active, open dialogue with all authorities to strengthen our partnership with Finland and local organisations."
results.summary:
Google has been ordered to halt construction on two Finnish datacentre sites after illegally clearcutting 400,000 trees without completing mandatory environmental impact assessments for the massive infrastructure project.

### Key Points
- The Finnish Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV) issued a stop-work order for Google sites in Muhos and Otanmäki earlier this month.
- Approximately 250,000 trees were felled in Muhos and 150,000 in Otanmäki before the company secured necessary environmental permits.
- Google’s €13 billion AI infrastructure project is the largest of its kind in Finland, aimed at leveraging the country's cool climate and stable energy grid.
- Over 93,000 people have signed a petition demanding stricter regulations and community compensation for the environmental damage caused by the clearcutting.
- Google has apologized for the incident, claiming it acted on a misunderstanding of local legislation, and has pledged to comply with all regulatory requirements.

### Why it Matters
The controversy has sparked a national debate in Finland regarding the environmental cost of hosting global tech infrastructure and the limited economic benefits provided to local communities. This incident is expected to become a significant political issue in the upcoming April elections as the government balances its desire for foreign investment against public concerns over environmental protection.

results.title: Bitcoin slides below $82,000 as AI doubts return, with DeFi tokens leading declines
results.author: Oliver Knight, Omkar Godbole
results.content:
Bitcoin slides below $82,000 as AI doubts return, with DeFi tokens leading declines
Bitcoin as much as 2.9% to around $81,600 as Nasdaq futures dropped, while the CoinDesk 80 lost 3.5% and DeFi index slid 6%.
- Bitcoin fell to around $81,800, down 2.7% since midnight UTC, extending its decline below $82,500 after a late-Wednesday surge to nearly $84,800 reversed.
- Mixed results from Tesla and Meta revived doubts over AI spending, weighing on equities and sending Nasdaq 100 futures down 1.32% and the Hang Seng index more than 2% lower.
- The CoinDesk DeFi index slumped 5.6% while the CoinDesk 5 fell 2.5%.
Bitcoin  slid by the most in two weeks, losing as much as 2.9% since midnight UTC to below $82,000 after mixed earnings reports from Tesla  and Meta Platforms  revived doubts over AI spending and sent equities lower in Asia.
Chinese stocks entered a bear market, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index fell more 3%, South Korea’s Kospi lost 3.5% and Japan’s Nikkei 225 slipped 2.7%. Nasdaq 100 index futures dropped 1.32% and S&P 500 futures 0.66%.
Altcoins fell even harder than bitcoin, with the CoinDesk 80 (CD80) recently down 3.2% compared with 2.5% for the CoinDesk 5 (CD5). Ether  lost 2.6% to near $2,400. DeFi bore the brunt, with the sector index (DFX) sliding 5.6%.
Spot bitcoin ETFs took in more than $1 billion over the first three days of the week, according to SoSoValue data, and Solana’s Alpenglow upgrade went live overnight, though SOL fell 2.4% to around $104. U.S. jobless claims are due later today.
Derivatives positioning
- Crypto futures see churn: Trading in crypto derivatives surged 19% to $226.6 billion, even as open interest fell 2.46% to $141.8 billion and liquidations jumped 52% to $431.1 million. Traders were mostly closing bets, not opening new ones. Longs and shorts are split almost evenly, so the pain was not one-sided.
- BTC and ETH, majors see no new money: Volume jumped 36% for bitcoin and 27% for ether, yet open interest fell about as much as price did. That means the number of contracts held barely changed, and the dollar drop in open interest is mostly price. Traders were active, but they were not adding or cutting risk in size. Funding is barely positive, so there is no crowded bet on either side.
- ZEC, NEAR, UNI, LINK and SUI, altcoin longs are leaving: Open interest fell much faster than price in all five coins. ZEC is the clearest case, with open interest dropping 6.99% as the price fell 2.34%. NEAR (-8.83%) and UNI (-10.17%) showed the same pattern. Positions are likely being closed, not held through the dip.
- XAU, XAUT, XAG and CL, traders pile into commodity perps: Money is flowing into commodity contracts while crypto drains. Open interest in gold rose 12% even as its price slipped, which implies about 13% more contracts. Tokenized gold XAUT (+10%) and silver (+6.8%) show the same pattern. Rising open interest with a falling price means traders are adding shorts, or longs are buying the dip and paying to hold. Crude oil open interest is up 6.29% with negative funding of -0.0126%, so shorts are paying to stay in.
- OI-normalized CVD shows market-order selling has taken over: Some 24 hours ago, almost every token saw more market-order buying than selling, with the gap peaking in the middle of the night. That flipped in the morning, with market-order selling dominating across major tokens, including BTC and ETH.
- XMR is the outlier on the funding rates heatmap: Monero funding at around an annualized 70% is far above every other token. It shows that longs are paying a steep premium to hold, which is the kind of leverage build-up CoinDesk flagged on Wednesday. It is the one pocket of crowding in an otherwise quiet market, so it is the token to watch for a liquidation event if the price turns.
- Implied volatility gauges stay near yearly lows: Bitcoin’s BVIV and ether’s EVIV are hovering just above their 2026 lows. Options traders are not paying for big price swings, which points to a calm market.
- Calls dominate volume on Deribit: The $85,000 and $86,000 calls expiring Oct. 30 were the most traded bets on Deribit over the past 24 hours. Short-dated skews still favor puts, so downside protection costs more than upside bets. It seems traders want to chase a rally, but are not prepared to drop their hedges. Ether options show the same pattern.
Token talk
- Privacy coins diverged, with monero (XMR) adding 4.9% to around $651, one of only five members of the CoinDesk 100 (CD100) to gain since midnight, while zcash (ZEC) fell 4.8% to around $1,252. XMR is up around 19% over the month, with futures open interest topping $300 million this week, near January’s record, according to SoSoValue data.
- DeFi led the decline on Thursday. Curve fell 8.2% to 37 cents, though it is still up around 4% over the week. Ethena (ENA) lost 7.2%, extending a decline of around 25% over the month from its late-September peak. Uniswap (UNI) dropped 5%, leaving it down around 20% in October despite record fee revenue in September, according to Token Terminal.
- Celestia (TIA) fell 3.7%, extending a slide of this week’s slide to 9% and trimming the month’s gain to around 31%, ahead of an unlock of 5.58 million TIA on Oct. 31. Layerzero lost 4.2% and worldcoin , the iris-scanning identity token, dropped 7.3%.
- Sandbox and starknet tumbled by 5.1% and 6.1%, respectively. SAND had advanced after South Korea’s Upbit, Bithumb and Coinone lifted trading cautions, while STRK had gained after the network said it was considering becoming a quantum-resistant layer-1.
- Pump.fun , the Solana memecoin launchpad token, fell 6.0% and remains down around 19% this month.

results.title: I'm the 25-year-old CEO of Lean In. I love my 2-minute cleaning hack, talking to myself on walks, and beach weekends — here's my routine.
results.author: Julia Pugachevsky
results.content:
This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Bridget Griswold, the 25-year-old CEO of Lean In, who lives in San Francisco. It's been edited for length and clarity.
I fell in love with technology at Brown University, where I studied computer science and business. I worked with two female professors to build a robot. I interned at a semiconductor manufacturing company and also loved design and art.
Product management felt like a really wonderful combination of all those interests, and that was my role at Meta a year after graduating from college. My team and I redesigned the Instagram search grid, so now when you search for large Instagram accounts, you're routed to the search results page rather than directly to those accounts. I'm very proud of that.
While at Meta, an incredible female mentor connected me to Sheryl Sandberg. Meeting her felt so surreal and is what led me to start my role as CEO at Lean In in March. It feels like a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to do mission-driven work.
I was a swimmer as a kid, and as my swim coach used to say: "You get out of swimming what you put into it." I think that applies to many things in life: The more you put in, the more you get out.
Here's a day in my life.
I wake up to my needy, angelic cat around 7:30 a.m.
The second I wake up, I pet my crying and whining cat. She's an angel but very needy.
I'm not a breakfast person, but I need coffee immediately. I have many cups of coffee throughout the day. One of the first things I do is make some at home.
I always tidy up my apartment while brushing my teeth
The most productive two minutes of my day are when I brush my teeth. I clean and tidy my apartment at the same time.
I'm probably not super focused on brushing my teeth, which is maybe a problem, but I'm also making my bed, emptying the dishwasher, feeding my cat, or starting the coffee maker.
I always move really quickly; I don't like to sit still. Brushing my teeth and standing still would make me antsy, so I like to get something else done at the same time.
I'm still adjusting to West Coast hours
I moved from New York City to San Francisco in August.
In New York, I went to Solidcore classes before work every day. Working on the West Coast, the workday starts earlier than on the East Coast, so I'm still learning whether I like to work out in the morning or after work.
When I take the bus to the office three days a week, I often use that time to catch up on personal housekeeping tasks like scheduling appointments or texting back my friends who live on the East Coast.
I come to the office around 8 a.m. or 8:30 a.m.
A majority of my in-person time is spent in meetings. As CEO, I enjoy being involved in all aspects of the team.
I'll meet with our content and research team — we spend a lot of time digging into data, such as some really exciting new research on trad wives in the manosphere. I also often meet with our product and tech team, as well as many of our partners, to help grow our programs.
We have lunch in the office — my favorite is a salad-plus-smoothie combo — and it's a really wonderful time to connect with the team.
I also love connecting with our Lean In community. One thing we're focused on is closing early gender gaps in AI usage. Our flagship program, Circles, consists of groups of 8 to 12 women who meet regularly to support each other in their careers — we have over 170,000 members. It's a perfect forum to hold each other accountable for upskilling in AI.
Every week, I send AI tips to our network leaders. A recent one encouraged the use of AI notetakers, as women are more likely to take notes during meetings and miss out on participating.
Lean In is in over 180 countries, and it's really heartwarming to see that our commitment to our mission has a positive impact on women's careers. Getting to speak with them is really energizing and rewarding.
I rehearse for meetings by talking to myself on walks
Another habit of mine I've been told is weird is how I prepare for big meetings.
If I have a presentation or interview coming up, I'll set up a Zoom and practice speaking to myself. Talking for a long time is sort of an unnatural act, and the first time you do it is probably not going to be your best.
Sometimes, I'll even go on a walk and wear headphones, pretending like I'm in a meeting or on a phone call, but I'm actually talking to myself and practicing.
When there's a bug, I usually fix the code myself
Because of my background in computer science, I spend a lot of my time finding bugs or things I believe we should change on our platform. I'll code and fix those on my own. Thankfully, with AI, it's so much faster to code now than it was a few years ago.
Our team is busy, and my goal is to enable everyone to have as much impact and move as quickly as possible. If I can help unblock the tech team or resolve an issue rather than add it to their plate, I'm always more than happy to do so.
I leave work around 6 p.m.
I continue to work until I go to bed pretty much every night.
It's nice to have that time at home, when I'm not running around between meetings, to focus, give feedback on documents the team has sent, write, respond to emails, and brainstorm my own ideas.
I take breaks to tidy up my apartment and make dinner. Living in New York got me out of the habit of cooking, so I'm taking the initiative to cook more meals, like rice bowls. I would say about half the time I order takeout, like pho, and the other half I cook, which is progress for me.
If my work doesn't require intense focus, I'll do it from the couch and put a happy TV show on, which right now is "Schitt's Creek." I think it's a nice balance between relaxation and getting things done.
I usually get in bed around 10:30 p.m.
I've been trying to make a habit of reading every night instead of going on my phone, which has been a really positive change. I like anything I read to be a distraction. I'm currently reading "Big Little Lies" and enjoying it.
It's nice to spend 30 minutes reading something like fantasy that's completely different from what I think about at work. That way, I'm not spinning on all the things I need to do or coming up with new ideas that can't get done in my sleep anyway.
Weekends are for the beach and farmers market
My boyfriend works in Los Angeles and flies up to San Francisco every weekend. We've made a tradition of going to the Fort Mason Farmers Market on Sundays for fresh produce to cook an at-home meal that night.
I also enjoy seeing friends over the weekend. My preference is to go on a long walk or go to the beach. I also enjoy fitting in some work — emails, deep-focus work, or reading — throughout the weekend.

results.title: iPhone Duo reviews: The absolute best foldable phone, but not without compromise
results.author: Ben Lovejoy
results.content:
We posted our own review of the iPhone Duo yesterday, and Chance Miller was left convinced that “this form factor represents the future of the iPhone,” while acknowledging that the first-gen iPhone Duo comes with trade-offs.
I think what surprised me most is the degree of consensus found across the reviews, given the generally polarized appeal of foldable phones. That’s not to say reviewers think everyone should buy one, but there is widespread agreement on the pros and cons – starting with five key takeouts …
Five key takeouts
First, all the reviews I’ve read and watched say that the iPhone Duo is hands-down the best foldable phone on the market. Apple waited a very long time before joining the foldable party, and it seems clear that it was absolutely right to do so.
Second, this phone is absolutely not for everyone. Even leaving aside the high purchase cost, the form factor currently involves compromises that would rule it out for some. If you expect to use the outer screen most of the time and only unfold it a few times a day, then the trade-offs of the heavy weight when held in one hand and the unusual display shape are just too big a drawback. This phone really only makes sense if you expect to make frequent use of the larger unfolded screen in your day-to-day use.
Third, Apple hasn’t made the crease invisible, and indeed has made no claims to do so. You can see it in certain lights at certain angles, and you can feel it when running your finger across the screen. But everyone agrees that this is the least intrusive crease ever seen on a foldable, and that it’s simply not an issue in real life use. More on this in a moment.
Fourth, a great many apps haven’t yet been updated, and in the worst case that means seeing an iPhone screen layout stranded in the middle of a mostly black inner display. The optimistic view is that this will rapidly change, but be prepared for some disappointments with third-party apps in early usage.
Finally, going back to Touch ID is a significant compromise after being used to Face ID. We do have to bear in mind that reviewers have only had a chance to use the device for a week, but certainly in that time most say they didn’t really get used to it and would absolutely prefer Face ID.
Fold testing
A couple of reviewers used machines to subject the iPhone Duo to thousands of folds and unfolds to test two things. Does the crease become significantly more visible over time, and how does the hinge hold up?
In both cases, there is a measurable impact. Joanna Stern’s tests found that the hinge is affected across tens of thousands of folds, but interestingly becomes stiffer rather than looser – the opposite of what we would expect. However, while this change was measurable using a strain gauge after 32,000 folds, she said she couldn’t feel it in normal use.
HTX Studio did the most scientific testing of the impact of thousands of folds on the crease. The depth of the crease when new was measured at just 48 microns, about half the thickness of a sheet of paper, while the slope of the crease measured at less than 0.1 degrees – both markedly better than competing foldables. After 3,000 folds, the depth of the crease increased to 167 microns and the slope increased to 1.24 degrees. That brings it more in line with the measurements of other foldables after the same number of tests.
The bottom line
There are links to the full reviews, but here is the bottom line from each …
After 20 years of iPhones that look mostly the same, it’s exciting to see Apple chart a new course. But the Duo is still one of the most early adopter Apple products I’ve tested in a long time. It’s easy to imagine what Gen 2 will look like. It’s lighter, there’s Face ID, a better camera inside, and hopefully a lower price. Also, it’s got a telephoto camera, and it’s no longer a hand warmer.
The good news is most of my other frustrations can be fixed with software updates and developers figuring out how to make great apps for two very different screen sizes. Sure, early adopters have to navigate some choppy waters, but as Apple developers catch up, I can see smoother sailing ahead.
Apple’s first attempt [at a foldable] brings plenty of fresh ideas with real purpose behind them that deserves credit. But think about it: these ideas mostly fix flaws built into the folding design rather than pushing the phone experience forward.
[Will this make foldables mainstream?] I still doubt it because this design has two fundamental conflicts at its core. First, the [aspect ratios] of two screens work against each other. Improve the outer screen and the inner screen becomes a big empty square. Favor the inner screen [as Apple has done] and the outer screen becomes a passport that’s hard to grip. It’s a zero-sum game. More importantly, whatever the balance, you get a makeshift phone outside and a cut down tablet inside. Neither delivers the best
experience.
Second, the benefits are occasional, but the cost are constant. To fit a hinge and the big screen, it sacrifices weight, battery life, cooling, performance, cameras, and most importantly, price. But use one or watch other people do and you’ll see they mostly use the outer screen […] You enjoy the benefits some of the time but pay the price all the time.
If you really want to do something, or sit back and read or watch something, the big display is fantastic. But that Duo-as-tablet experience is so cumbersome compared to the “just look at it” experience of using a regular iPhone uno that you simply cannot do it every time you use the Duo. You will use the outer display quite a bit. And using the outer display delivers the worst iPhone experience ever. I mean, some iPhone has to be the one that offered the worst iPhone experience ever. That iPhone is the outer half of the iPhone Duo […]
If you’d rather trade your iPhone for an iPad Mini that you can fold in half to carry around, the iPhone Duo might be the form factor for you. Even if that’s the case, though, this first iPhone Duo might not suit you, for all the various irritations and shortcomings I’ve documented […] It’s been a lot of fun trying the Duo out for a week, but it feels like I’ve gotten to use an extraordinarily polished prototype — not a finished product that I’d want to buy and carry.
CNET:
Aside from some minor shortcomings, Apple appears to have stuck the landing with its long-awaited foldable. Hopefully, future iterations will add elements such as Face ID while improving the camera capabilities, either by adding a telephoto lens or bolstering the inner screen’s FaceTime camera. It would be nice to see multitasking become more dynamic in the future, too.
[But] most people just don’t need a phone that doubles as a tablet. [While the Duo] is a foldable experience that feels cohesive, intuitive and genuinely useful, which could help win over more people to foldables in general, I think that broader appeal is still a ways off.
Whether you’re an iPhone fan, foldable evangelist, or Android user who’s just been waiting to see what Apple offers, I think we can all agree that the iPhone Duo has already achieved what competing foldables have not been able to in seven years: generate considerable buzz for foldable phones […] This is what we’ve been waiting for after more than a decade of matured bar-style phones. Finally, phone hardware and software are genuinely exciting again, which is something to celebrate […]
As for whether you should get the iPhone Duo—that depends on if you can afford it, either buying it outright, paying in installments, or leasing it through the Apple Upgrade program. Do you want a foldable phone, and why? Will you use the larger screen often, and how much value will you get from it? Will the weight bother you? Do you need better cameras? There are so many personal factors to consider before you decide. The iPhone Duo isn’t the “definitive” iPhone to own. Apple’s iPhone lineup now caters to every budget and every type of user. Only you can be honest with yourself about your needs.
Top comment by sean roberts
The absolute best foldable? Not sure which videos you watch but from what I can see, the phone is too heavy and needs the software to catch up. If this was a Android phone, you guys would be calling it the worst phone ever that nobody will buy. It has potential but I suspect a lot of the pre orders will be returned by customers who expect it to work great straight away. Not every buyer will want to wait for the devs to catch up, which they will but it will take some time.
The iPhone Duo is the best designed foldable phone I’ve ever tested, with a sturdy and premium build and a nano-texture display that hides the crease. I also like the multiple usage modes and split-screen multitasking. However, while fully updated apps for the Duo look great, non-optimized apps do not. And the lack of a telephoto zoom is a bummer for a $2,000 phone […]
I like the iPhone Duo’s nano texture display in that it greatly reduces glare outdoors and minimizes the crease better than any foldable I’ve tested. But you give up perfect blacks with this matte panel and more saturated colors versus the iPhone 18 Pro Max. You also sacrifice a telephoto lens and Face ID. I can live with those trade-offs, but that doesn’t mean I like them.
In a way it’s a good thing that the iPhone Duo is backordered for many until December or January. That will give developers plenty of time to update their offerings for this foldable. I don’t think it will take that long, though, based on the high demand.
Overall, though, I think the iPhone Duo is the best designed foldable yet with the most polished, intuitive and fun software experience.
This is often the case with first-generation products, but it may be prudent to wait for the Duo 2—not because there are glaring issues but because I suspect Apple may tackle the weight problem with the next version, just as Samsung did on its latest iteration.
Folding phones will never be for everyone. Some people do not care for the bigger screen. Others have durability concerns, and a device with more moving parts will never be as repairable or robust as its single-slab counterpart. Price is a barrier for others—but, on that note, the Duo is surprisingly on par with its competitors (though still expensive).
But the folding category is here to stay. I know people who swear by the fold and won’t buy anything else. I’m starting to convert, especially with the newer passport-style shape. Now if only someone could figure out how to put a real zoom camera on there.
There’s a lot of potential in the Duo, but right now it is a first-gen device in every possible way. It is expensive, it’s full of compromises, and it can be incredibly frustrating to use. Switching from the Duo back to one of our standard slab phones to get something done often felt like a relief […] But all of the risk and weirdness of the Duo is also fun, in the way the best early adopter devices are fun. It’s incomplete as a product, but complete enough as an idea that you can see where things are going […]
We’ll see what happens with the Duo, but as it stands, it is very much an open question whether Apple made the right choices about the Duo’s screen sizes and aspect ratios. Most Duo owners will find that the cover display is simply too small to use all the time […] Apple also made some very real compromises around the camera […]
But the Duo is a more cohesive idea about foldables than most of its Android competition, precisely because Apple has a better app and developer story to lean on. Right now the problem for most Android foldables is that the inner screens aren’t that useful so there’s no super compelling reason to open them. The problem with the Duo is that the outer screen isn’t useful enough, so you want to open it all the time […] The real answer is somewhere in the middle — for both screens to be interesting and useful. Someone’s going to get there, and we’ll see if Apple can be the first.
What’s your take after reading the review conclusions? Have the reviews made you more or less interested in the iPhone Duo? Please share your thoughts in the comments.
results.summary:
The new iPhone Duo has received widespread praise as the most polished foldable smartphone available, though reviewers highlight significant trade-offs regarding weight, camera capabilities, and software optimization.

### Key Points
- The iPhone Duo features a refined hinge and a nano-texture display that minimizes the screen crease more effectively than competing foldable devices.
- Early adopters face compromises, including the absence of Face ID, a lack of a telephoto lens, and limited third-party app optimization for the dual-screen layout.
- Stress testing by HTX Studio showed the crease depth increases from 48 microns to 167 microns after 3,000 folds, while hinges may become stiffer over time.
- Critics note that the device’s aspect ratio forces users to choose between a narrow outer screen or a tablet-like inner display, creating a zero-sum user experience.
- High demand has led to backorders extending into December and January, providing developers additional time to update applications for the unique form factor.

### Why it Matters
The iPhone Duo represents Apple’s first entry into the foldable market, signaling a major shift in the company's hardware strategy after years of standard slab-style designs. While the device generates significant industry buzz, its status as a first-generation product suggests that mainstream adoption may depend on future iterations addressing weight, battery life, and camera limitations.

results.title: UK working to identify exposure after global cyber-security warning
results.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
results.content:
- Published
The UK government says it is working to identify any potential exposure in its online services, after critical cyber-security flaws were identified in the PHP programming language that underpins a significant number of the world's websites.
Governments and some of the world's biggest companies are rushing to protect systems that use PHP before hackers can exploit the flaws.
The flaws were first discovered by AI, after which governments urged anyone who uses PHP to address them.
A UK government spokesperson urged "all organisations, private and public, large and small" to follow guidance to protect their systems.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as well as its counterparts in the EU and Australia, earlier urged those who use PHP to apply the fixes.
"Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," the NCSC said in a statement., external
Amazon said its threat intelligence system identified it was targeted on Saturday. It added there were further "exploitation attempts" once the embargo on the flaw warning was lifted.
The company said it "automatically detected and restricted malicious scanning attempts targeting this vulnerability."
PHP powers a vast number of platforms, including online shops, Wikipedia and WordPress – the content management system behind many websites like blogs.
When you visit a website like Wikipedia, PHP is the code that collects information you need and presents it in a way you can read on the web.
Surrey Centre for Cyber Security Prof Alan Woodward said the flaw affects some 30 million websites.
As well as the scale of the flaw, Woodward said the nature of it means "an attacker can get their own code on to the webserver and run it and basically do whatever they like."
"They can steal data , they can go to other parts of your network. All sort of things like that - even plant a backdoor to get in later on, so it's pretty serious," Woodward told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
Cyber security researcher Ryan Austin, who has been researching PHP security for the last 20 years, said he discovered the flaw in the programming language.
He told the Today programme it was "the most serious vulnerability I've ever found" which "started with a hunch that I would not have been able to scratch without AI".
Austin described PHP as "one of the first web languages that powered the early internet".
"It's in a lot of places that you wouldn't expect to be that are basically very core to how the internet runs in a lot of ways. It's like all the old things that are in a house that you know keeps it [running] but you don't really think about," the PHP researcher said.
But Austin said this incident is not necessarily bad news because organisations would now "run and patch PHP immediately" if they haven't already.
Amazon announced on Wednesday that it had identified a "PHP2Shell exploitation attempt" that occurred on 17 October.
In the attack, an anonymous internet address attempted to target weaknesses in one of Amazon's decoy or "honeypot" systems, the company's security chief CJ Moses said.
The use of an anonymous IP address suggests that the activity was conducted by a "threat actor", he said.
While the PHP Foundation intended to release its discovery later this month along with a complete fix for the problem, usually referred to by software developers as a "patch", details of the flaw were leaked on social media on Tuesday.
In subsequent attacks on Amazon that occurred on 21 October, "the actual payloads and choices in anonymisation infrastructure varied, suggesting these were multiple actors," Moses said.
The attacks occurred after the leak, but before the embargo was lifted on the PHP warning.
The use of AI means that "more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed", Moses added.
The PHP incident has "demonstrated how quickly AI is changing our cybersecurity landscape", Australian Council on AI Strategy CEO Anna-Maria Arabia told the BBC, as "what used to take months, to expose a vulnerability, is now taking days".
She warned that threats would only become more commonplace as AI technology rapidly improves. It is "not going backwards, in other words", she said.
The PHP flaws went undetected for at least a decade.
Cyber-security firm Wiz has estimated that "roughly 70%" of the internet is affected, though the BBC is unable to independently verify that figure.
The websites for several BBC programmes including Doctor Who and The Traitors are currently inaccessible.
They have not confirmed a link to PHP - BBC News has approached them for comment.
The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said it had followed guidance to take its website offline, "in view of the critical security issues affecting PHP".
Edinburgh and Oxford council websites also went offline on Wednesday, but are now accessible.
The Dutch cybersecurity agency went offline as a precaution, and Finland's government shut down its public web services. Wikipedia also took down parts of its website.
This was in line with advice issued by governments, including the US, to take websites down if the flaws could not immediately be fixed.
The US National Security Agency said that the vulnerabilities identified "often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database".
It could allow attackers to "steal sensitive data, disrupt services, or move deeper into a network. These vulnerabilities are flaws in PHP itself, not in the hosted application or its configuration," the NSA said in a later update.
OpenAI called the discovery, "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".
results.summary:
The UK government and global organizations are rushing to patch critical security flaws in the PHP programming language that potentially expose millions of websites to malicious cyberattacks.

### Key Points
- Researcher Ryan Austin discovered the critical PHP vulnerability, which had remained undetected for at least a decade.
- The flaw allows attackers to execute unauthorized code, steal sensitive data, or plant backdoors on affected web servers.
- Amazon reported detecting and blocking multiple "PHP2Shell" exploitation attempts targeting its systems following a premature leak of the vulnerability details.
- Government agencies in the UK, EU, Australia, and Finland have advised organizations to apply patches immediately or take vulnerable systems offline.
- Estimates suggest the vulnerability impacts a significant portion of the internet, including major platforms like Wikipedia and WordPress.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the growing role of artificial intelligence in both discovering complex software vulnerabilities and enabling attackers to exploit them rapidly. Because PHP underpins a vast segment of the global web infrastructure, these flaws pose a systemic risk to data security and service availability for both public and private sectors.

results.title: Google’s Illyes: Robots.txt Covers Crawling, Not AI Training via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
results.author: Matt G. Southern
results.content:
Robots.txt, as the internet standard RFC 9309 defines it, governs which URLs a crawler may request, not what happens to the content afterward, Google’s Gary Illyes said in a Search Central video published Wednesday. To keep one AI crawler out while allowing others, he said, you have to target that crawler’s user-agent token in the file.
The video is the second episode of The Non-Canonical Cabinet, where Illyes and Cherry Prommawin of Google Search Relations take edge-case questions from the community. Illyes is also co-author, with Mozilla’s Martin Thomson, of an IETF Internet-Draft that would give robots.txt a standard way to state usage preferences. Prommawin recommended writing non-English rule paths in percent-encoded form for crawlers other than Google’s.
What Illyes Said About AI Training
The episode’s question was whether robots.txt can allow AI crawling of a website and keep that same information out of generative model training. According to Illyes, “So as defined by RFC 9309, robots.txt is an access preference protocol.” He went on to say robots.txt “doesn’t dictate what a system does with the data after it has already crawled it.” If you want to completely block a specific AI crawler from accessing your entire website, Illyes stated, you need to “target their specific user agent tokens explicitly in the file.”
The episode illustrated a fictional directive (e.g., No-AI-Chicken-Training) which was shown on-screen and would be ignored by a parser. Google’s robots.txt specification page states that the four elements supported are User-Agent, Allow, Disallow, and Sitemap; invalid lines will be ignored by Google.
As for RFC 9309 specifically (Section 2.2.4), it allows crawlers to decide how they’ll process a record outside the scope of this protocol. Therefore, whether or not an additional line accomplishes something depends on the crawler interpreting it.
What Google-Extended Controls
Google-Extended is a robots.txt token with no user agent of its own. Google crawls under its existing user agents, and Google’s list of common crawlers says the token is “used in a control capacity.” It manages whether content Google crawls can be used to train future Gemini models and for grounding in Gemini Apps and Grounding with Google Search on Vertex AI. The page says it doesn’t affect a site’s inclusion in Google Search and isn’t a ranking signal.
Google-Extended’s meaning as a usage control comes from Google’s documentation for its own products, rather than RFC 9309. The hosts didn’t discuss it on air, but the video’s description links to the same list.
The Draft That Would Add A Usage Rule
The current version of the IETF draft Illyes co-wrote, dated Aug. 19, would update RFC 9309, if approved, with a Content-Usage rule for robots.txt and a matching HTTP header. Neither the episode nor its description mentions the draft.
Under the draft, Allow and Disallow would continue to govern which URLs can be crawled. Content-Usage would then define preferences as to how crawled content should be used. Those preferences would only relate to paths where a crawler has permission to fetch content. A Content-Usage field of “train-ai=n” is added to the draft’s example robots.txt file, which allows crawling.
The draft is still a Working Group Document. At present, its IETF Datatracker entry shows that the Working Group has not yet submitted the document for review by the IETF’s Steering Group (IESG). The Working Group’s planned date for sending it to the IESG was Aug. 2026. The ‘train-ai’ Label referenced above appears in a separate Vocabulary Draft, dated Sept. 14. That document states that it reflects no consensus within the Working Group.
Percent-Encode Non-English Paths
Cherry Prommawin’s advice for paths with non-English characters or emoji was that “you should use the encoded version in your robots.txt rules.” Google’s parser handles raw characters by encoding them, she said, but “other or older crawlers on the web might get confused.”
The on-screen example labeled a raw emoji path “Works for Google, might break others” and its percent-encoded form “The Safe, Standard Way.” Google’s spec page says its parser treats raw UTF-8 and percent-encoded paths the same way, and RFC 9309’s grammar allows UTF-8 characters in paths.
Why This Matters
The method you would need in robots.txt to limit AI use of your content while keeping your site visible in Google Search depends on what bot or product you are working with. Disallow statements may prevent specific AI crawlers from accessing particular webpages. For Gemini, the documented control of Google is Google-Extended and includes both training and grounding. There currently is no standard way of expressing a training preference independent of the bots allowed to crawl the webpage; one exists only as a draft.
Websites that use URLs with languages other than English will want to encode their robots.txt paths using percent encoding. Percent encoding is safer because, although Google treats both raw and encoded versions of the same robots.txt rule path equally, other crawlers could potentially interpret raw characters differently.
Looking Ahead
According to the video description, the next Non-Canonical Cabinet episode will cover the 404 status code. The current Content-Usage draft is set to expire on Feb. 20, 2027, unless a new revision replaces it sooner.

results.summary:
Google’s Gary Illyes clarified that the robots.txt protocol only governs URL access and cannot restrict how AI models use data once it has been successfully crawled.

### Key Points
- The RFC 9309 standard defines robots.txt as an access preference protocol, not a tool for controlling post-crawl data usage by AI systems.
- To block specific AI crawlers, website owners must explicitly target the crawler’s unique user-agent token within their robots.txt file.
- Google-Extended is a specific token used to manage whether Google crawls content for training Gemini models or for grounding in Vertex AI.
- An IETF Internet-Draft co-authored by Illyes proposes a new "Content-Usage" rule, though it is not yet an official standard and lacks industry consensus.
- Cherry Prommawin recommends using percent-encoded paths for non-English characters in robots.txt to ensure compatibility with older or non-Google web crawlers.

### Why it Matters
Website owners currently lack a universal standard to prevent AI training while still allowing search engine indexing, forcing them to rely on specific bot-by-bot exclusions. This technical limitation highlights the growing gap between existing web protocols and the complex data-usage requirements of modern generative artificial intelligence.

results.title: ‘VPNs at Risk’: Tech Coalition Pushes Back on Piracy Blocking Duties for VPNs
results.author: Ernesto Van der Sar
results.content:
When Rep. Darrell Issa introduced his site blocking bill last month, VPN providers made the list.
The American Copyright Protection Act (ACPA) would allow courts to order ISPs, DNS resolvers, and VPNs to block foreign pirate sites.
The competing DEFEND IP Act, introduced days later by Rep. Zoe Lofgren and Sen. Thom Tillis, does the opposite. It explicitly excludes services that only offer VPNs.
The VPN industry has a voice in U.S. blocking debates through the Internet Infrastructure Coalition (i2Coalition). In addition to representing companies such as Amazon, Cloudflare, and Google, the group runs a VPN Trust Initiative, with ExpressVPN, NordVPN, and Surfshark as founding members.
The coalition has been relatively quiet in recent site blocking discussions, but today, on Global Encryption Day, i2Coalition published a report titled “VPNs at Risk.”
Like last year’s DNS at Risk report, it warns against turning neutral infrastructure into a copyright enforcement tool.
From Pirate Sites to VPNs
Copyright enforcement is one of the reasons governments consider regulating VPNs, the report notes. VPNs can be used to bypass blocking measures and may make it harder for rightsholders to identify infringers or enforce geographic licensing restrictions.
France has been one of the prime examples of this type of regulation, i2Coalition notes. In May 2025, a Paris court ordered NordVPN, CyberGhost, Surfshark, ExpressVPN, and Proton VPN to block 203 pirate sports streaming domains at the request of Canal+.
“These cases, brought by rightsholders before French courts, illustrate how obligations imposed at one layer of the Internet can migrate to another when users find alternative technical paths around court-ordered restrictions,” the report notes.
That raises a broader question.
According to the report, the issue is not just which intermediaries can be ordered to block, but whether these measures actually reduce piracy, and what side effects they have for lawful users.
The French legal battle isn’t over either.
The report describes the decisions as “currently pending appeal,” but it doesn’t mention the latest twists. On September 30, the Paris Court of Appeal put an appeal by NordVPN, Proton, and CyberGhost against a similar order, obtained by football league LFP, on hold. It will first wait for a ruling from France’s Supreme Court, the Cour de cassation, in related DNS blocking cases.
A week later, the Paris court refused beIN’s request for daily penalties against VPN providers and Cloudflare, which had not fully blocked the targeted sites.
i2Coalition is aware of these developments but will keep the report text as is.
“We’re following those proceedings, including the pending Cour de cassation outcome. We’re keeping the text for this release, but those developments will inform future updates. They don’t change our broader concern about the implications of extending blocking obligations to VPN providers,” Executive Director Christian Dawson tells us.
Target the Right Layer
The report doesn’t ask for a VPN exemption from any and all regulation. Instead, it urges lawmakers to be precise, and to take measures where they make the most sense.
“Policymakers should consider where meaningful knowledge and control actually reside and whether an obligation can be directed toward the relevant conduct or service before moving deeper into general-purpose Internet infrastructure. The further an intervention moves from the activity being regulated, the greater the need to consider its effects on unrelated users and services,” the report reads.
Targeting the right layer is particularly important when it comes to VPNs. Consumer VPN services and corporate networks rely on many of the same underlying technologies, including protocols such as OpenVPN and WireGuard.
The report notes that Russia’s reported blocking of these VPN protocols shows how hard it is to tell the different uses apart at the network level.
When it comes to liability, i2Coalition points to the U.S. Supreme Court’s Cox ruling from earlier this year. This ruling confirmed that continuing to provide an Internet service, while knowing that some customers may misuse it, isn’t enough on its own to establish contributory copyright infringement.
The group sees the principles from this ruling as relevant to VPNs as well, but it doesn’t claim the matter is settled.
“If providers face liability merely because general-purpose services can be misused, they may have strong incentives to terminate users, restrict access, or intervene preemptively even when they have limited knowledge of the underlying conduct. Obligations should therefore reflect what an intermediary can reasonably know, control, and address,” the report warns.
“We see those principles as relevant to the debate around VPNs, but we aren’t suggesting that the ruling automatically determines the outcome of every VPN case. That would depend on the facts and legal issues presented,” Dawson notes.
VPN providers are not completely without responsibilities. According to the report, they can strengthen trust through independent audits and cooperation with legitimate legal processes. Voluntary programs, such as the VPN Trust Initiative’s own Trust Seal, can complement these efforts.
Lawmakers, in turn, should involve VPN providers and other technical experts from the start when they want to tackle a problem.
Silent on U.S. Bills
The report doesn’t apply these recommendations to the pending site blocking bills, as neither ACPA nor DEFEND IP is mentioned.
That’s notable, as ACPA would allow courts to name VPN providers with 100,000 or more monthly U.S. users or subscribers in a blocking order. That’s a position VPN companies would rather not be in.
TorrentFreak asked i2Coalition why the report doesn’t mention the two bills. Dawson says that the group is following both proposals, but that this particular report focuses on other developments.
“For this edition, we’ve focused on the developments covered in the report rather than trying to capture every pending legislative proposal. We expect to revisit US legislation in a future update as the debate develops,” Dawson says.
For now, both bills remain pending. Issa retires at the end of the year and Tillis’s term ends in January, so both bills would have to move ahead before the current session closes.
—
A copy of i2Coalition’s “VPNs at Risk” report is available here (pdf).
results.summary:
The i2Coalition released a new report warning that forcing VPN providers to block pirate websites threatens neutral internet infrastructure and risks harming legitimate users and corporate networks.

### Key Points
- The "VPNs at Risk" report argues against using general-purpose internet infrastructure as a tool for copyright enforcement.
- French courts recently ordered major providers, including NordVPN and ExpressVPN, to block pirate sports streaming domains.
- Legal appeals regarding these blocking orders are currently pending before France’s Supreme Court, the Cour de cassation.
- The report highlights that VPNs share underlying technologies with corporate networks, making it difficult to restrict traffic without collateral damage.
- U.S. legislative proposals like the American Copyright Protection Act (ACPA) could mandate that VPNs with over 100,000 users implement site-blocking measures.

### Why it Matters
This debate highlights a growing tension between copyright enforcement efforts and the preservation of a neutral, open internet. If lawmakers successfully mandate blocking at the VPN level, it could set a precedent that forces infrastructure providers to monitor and restrict user traffic, potentially undermining privacy and security for all users.

The criteria for judging the best AC units cover the basics of what you need when it’s 80 degrees with 100% humidity at four in the morning: How fast and how cool does this machine make your space, and how likely is it that you’ll be awoken by its intolerable noise? How user-friendly were the controls?
