results.title: the hidden landscape of the digital world: what it takes to keep technology running
results.author: thomai tsimpou I designboom
results.content:
[FEATURED]
the ‘cloud’ is physical: the hidden infrastructure behind digital life
The digital world is often described as immaterial, a space of information that moves invisibly between devices and across networks. The term ‘cloud,’ for instance, suggests an ethereal space where data like photos, images and more can be stored without occupying any tangible place. In reality, though, these files reside on physical servers housed in data centers, supported by networks, cooling systems, and energy infrastructure. Every search, video stream, and artificial intelligence query depends on systems that consume energy, water, land, and raw materials. From mineral extraction and semiconductor manufacturing to data centers and electronic waste, the infrastructure behind digital life has a substantial environmental footprint.
As demand for computation increases, we need to reconsider how these systems are designed and what their growth requires from the planet and humanity. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), data centers consumed approximately 485 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025. The agency projects that this figure could approach 950 terawatt-hours by 2030, driven in part by the expansion of artificial intelligence and other computationally intensive services. These figures reveal the growing physical demands behind technologies that are often presented detached from material reality. They also raise a fundamental question: can the digital economy become more sustainable if the infrastructure supporting it continues to expand?
the material origins of computation
The environmental footprint of digital technology begins before a device is switched on. Smartphones, computers, servers, and networking equipment depend on minerals extracted, processed, and transported through global supply chains. Copper carries electricity and data through physical networks, while other metals and specialized materials are used in circuit boards, batteries, and semiconductor components. Their extraction can require substantial energy and water, while mining and processing can disrupt landscapes and generate pollution. Electrification, transport, and renewable energy systems depend on mineral-intensive supply chains. However, the rapid expansion of digital infrastructure adds another source of demand, particularly as data centers require large quantities of servers and supporting equipment.
Semiconductor manufacturing introduces another layer of environmental complexity. Producing advanced chips involves highly controlled industrial environments, energy-intensive processes, and significant water requirements. A 2023 study examining environmental disclosures from 28 semiconductor companies reported approximately 789 million cubic meters of water withdrawals and 149 billion kilowatt-hours of energy consumption across the companies surveyed. These figures do not represent the entire global semiconductor industry, but they illustrate the scale of the resources involved in manufacturing the components that make modern computing possible.
data centers as physical architecture
Data centers house the servers that store and process the information we access every day. They require a lot of supporting infrastructure, from backup power systems to cooling equipment that prevents the machines from overheating. Where these facilities are built matters. Their location affects the availability of electricity and water, while the design of their cooling systems influences how much of each resource they consume. As more data centers are built to meet growing demand, their impact on local infrastructure becomes harder to ignore. Cooling is particularly important because computing equipment converts much of the electricity it uses into heat. That heat must be removed to maintain reliable operating conditions, creating an additional energy demand. Depending on the facility and its climate, cooling may rely on mechanical refrigeration, air-based systems, liquid cooling, or combinations of different technologies.
Even if a data center uses energy efficiently, it can still put pressure on the local electricity grid or consume water that is already in demand by nearby communities. The impact depends partly on where the facility is built and what resources are available there. A cooling system that works well in one location may be less suitable in another, particularly in areas where water is scarce. The location of a data center, its energy supply, and the way it is cooled are just as important as the technology inside it. These decisions are often made long before the servers start running, but they can determine how the facility affects its surroundings for years to come.
when efficiency is not enough
More efficient servers and cooling systems can reduce the energy needed to run a data center, but they do not necessarily reduce its total consumption. As computing capacity grows and new applications emerge, demand can rise faster than efficiency improves. This is particularly relevant to artificial intelligence, which requires computing power both to train models and to run them for users. As these services become more widely available, the amount of computation they require increases, even as the hardware becomes more efficient.
A data center may use less electricity to process each request but still consume more energy overall if it handles many more requests. The distinction matters when assessing the environmental impact of digital technology. Efficiency gains are useful, but they tell only part of the story. Total electricity consumption, water use, and demand on local infrastructure also need to be considered. The same applies to renewable energy. Using renewable electricity can reduce emissions associated with the power supply of a data center, but it does not address every part of its environmental footprint. The facility still requires land, construction materials, servers, and cooling systems, while the manufacture and eventual disposal of its equipment carry their own costs.
water, heat, and the possibilities of reuse
Water consumption is one of the most widely discussed environmental concerns surrounding data centers, particularly in regions already facing water shortages. Some facilities rely on water-based cooling to prevent servers from overheating, although consumption varies depending on the cooling system, climate, and operating conditions. Choosing where to build a data center is closely tied to the availability of local resources. Cooling systems also involve trade-offs. Air-based cooling, liquid cooling, and other approaches differ in their energy requirements, water consumption, and operating costs. No single solution works best in every setting, making local climate and resource availability important factors in the design of these facilities.
Heat is another part of the equation. Data centers generate large amounts of waste heat, which is usually removed from the building and released into the environment. In some cases, this heat can be recovered and used to warm nearby buildings or supply district heating networks, turning an operational by-product into a potential energy source. A 2024 study examined the potential for integrating data center waste heat into a district heating system in Italy. In the modeled scenarios, recovered heat supplied between 12 and 59 percent of the district heating mix, while gas consumption fell by approximately 11 to 58 percent. These figures represent modeled outcomes rather than measured savings from an operating facility, but they illustrate the potential benefits of connecting data centers to existing heating infrastructure. Unlike cooling, which is primarily concerned with managing the heat generated by servers, heat recovery looks at how that energy might be put to use. Its feasibility depends on factors such as the temperature of the recovered heat, the distance to potential users, and whether demand for heating coincides with its availability.
the problem of electronic waste
The environmental cost of digital technology continues after equipment leaves service. Servers, computers, phones, and networking hardware contain materials that can be recovered, but they also include components and substances that make safe processing difficult. When electronics are discarded without appropriate collection and treatment, valuable resources are lost and harmful materials can enter the environment. The Global E-waste Monitor 2024 reported that the world generated 62 billion kilograms of electronic waste in 2022. Only 22.3 percent of that total was documented as formally collected and recycled in an environmentally sound manner. The report projects that global e-waste could reach 82 billion kilograms by 2030.
Data centers regularly replace servers and other equipment to meet performance and reliability requirements. Newer hardware can process more information using less energy per task, but manufacturing it also requires new materials and energy. Whether replacing older equipment reduces the overall environmental impact depends on how much energy is saved during operation and what it takes to produce the replacement. Keeping equipment in use for longer can help reduce the need for new hardware. Servers that can be repaired, upgraded, and maintained are less likely to need replacing as soon as their performance begins to fall behind. When equipment reaches the end of its useful life, recycling can recover some of its materials for future use, although recycling alone does not address the resources required to manufacture new devices in the first place. Extending the life of working equipment, repairing components where possible, and recovering materials when equipment can no longer be used all have a role in reducing electronic waste.
designing for a less extractive digital future
Reducing the environmental impact of digital technology involves more than making servers faster or data centers more energy-efficient. It also means looking at where facilities are built, how they are cooled and powered, how long equipment remains in use, and what happens to it when it is replaced. Recovering waste heat, using renewable electricity, and designing equipment that can be repaired or reused can all help, but their benefits depend on how these measures are put into practice.
For architects and designers, data centers raise questions that go beyond the buildings themselves. Their energy and water needs affect the places where they operate, while their construction and equipment depend on materials sourced from elsewhere. Decisions about location, infrastructure, and maintenance can have consequences long after a facility is built. There is also the question of how much computing we actually need. As artificial intelligence and other digital services continue to expand, improving efficiency will not necessarily reduce overall resource use. The growing demand for computation deserves as much attention as the technologies developed to meet it. The cloud may feel distant from the physical world, but its infrastructure is not. It exists in mines, factories, warehouses, power stations, and data centers, all drawing on resources and leaving an environmental footprint. Recognizing this is a starting point for thinking differently about digital technology, not as something separate from the environment, but as part of it.

These stories rethink our relationship with the planet through interspecies architecture, living materials, regenerative landscapes and emerging technologies – learn more here! The chapter is presented in partnership with INDX|GLOBAL – a global cultural platform placing Indian architecture, design, and creative intelligence in conversation with the world.
Each designboom editorial series explores one theme in depth through projects, interviews, features and news across architecture, design, art and technology. Discover more chapters here, and get in touch if you’d like to submit a story through our submissions portal or contact form.

results.title: Why Are Modern Workspaces Ditching Traditional Office Chairs? These 9 Computer Chair Designs Offer Some Inspiration
results.author: Trendir Editorial Staff
results.content:
The chair you sit in all day shapes more than your posture. The best computer chairs figure out one thing well: keeping your back happy, matching the room, or making the hours feel shorter. These 9 ideas pull from a bunch of different setups so you can see what might actually work in yours.
If you work from home, the chair matters more than almost anything else in the room. The one you pick decides whether you’ll be shifting around every twenty minutes or actually getting things done, and whether the room looks pulled-together or like you grabbed whatever was on sale.
The chairs here cover a lot of ground: ergonomic workhorses, classic executive looks, cozy fabric picks, and a few that split the difference. Here’s what caught our eye.
Mesh backs breathe in a way that padded chairs can’t, which is why your back doesn’t start sticking to the chair by 3pm. The green seat is doing the design work here, giving a clean office actual personality without going overboard. If you work from home full-time, this is the kind of chair that earns its spot in the room.
This is the boardroom classic scaled down for a home office. The ribbed cushions and chrome base read as finished and intentional, not something you’d apologize for on a video call. It pairs well with wood desks and traditional home office setups where a gaming chair would look completely out of place.
Not every job needs a hard ergonomic shell. This one leans into cushioning: the padded wings, the headrest, the rounded armrests. It fits the kind of workday that’s less typing and more thinking, reading, or taking long calls where you want to lean back and actually relax.
Boucle (that nubby white fabric you’ve probably seen on couches lately) on a desk chair might sound impractical, but in a room that’s already personal and lived-in it just works. The pull-out ottoman is the real move, because standing up from a desk chair every two hours is overrated. Great for a makeup corner or a creative setup.
You can have a traditional office with bookshelves and a rug and still get a proper ergonomic chair. This one keeps the mesh back and lumbar support but ditches the aggressive gamer-chair shape. The soft beige means it fades into the room instead of fighting it, which is exactly what you want when the rest of the room has character.
Built for people who are in the chair before anyone else and still there at night. Thick padding, high back, headrest, and leather that holds up for years. The quilted detail is where it earns the executive label without going too flashy. Not a small chair, so check your desk and floor space before you commit.
A chair this color could easily look like a toy, but the clean lines and white frame keep it on the right side of grown-up. The footrest tucks away when you don’t need it, which is a feature you don’t appreciate until you’ve worked an eight-hour day without one. Smart pick if the rest of your modern chair setup already has personality.
One chair behind the desk, two in front, all matching. This is the setup for people who sometimes have clients over, or who just want the room to look like an office. The chrome bases and black leather keep it professional, and the matching set across the room makes the space feel finished instead of pieced together.
This blurs the line between office chair and lounge chair in the best way. Tufted back, armrests you could nap on, a side footrest that pulls out when the workday is done. Makes sense if your workspace is also where you unwind on weekends, and the cream fabric keeps everything soft without reading as fussy.
Which of these chairs feels most like something you’d actually want to work in?

Selecting the right home office chair is essential for maintaining productivity and comfort, with various designs ranging from ergonomic mesh models to stylish executive seating options available.

### Key Points

- Executive-style chairs featuring chrome bases and leather upholstery offer a professional aesthetic suitable for client-facing home offices.
- Ergonomic designs with lumbar support can be integrated into traditional home decor by choosing neutral colors like beige.
- Specialized features such as pull-out ottomans and tufted cushioning cater to creative workspaces and multi-purpose rooms.
- Padded, high-back leather chairs are engineered for durability and comfort during extended hours of continuous use.

### Why it Matters
Choosing the correct chair directly impacts physical health and daily work efficiency for remote professionals. Investing in a seat that balances ergonomic support with interior design ensures a functional workspace that remains comfortable throughout the entire workday.

results.title: Prolo Ring Lets You Click and Scroll Without a Mouse
results.author: Ida Torres
results.content:
There are days when you work on just your laptop. And then there are days when you have to switch between different devices and therefore also use different controllers. If you have a huge desk or workspace, then that’s probably fine. But if you’re working in a limited space, then the different controllers add to the clutter. What if you have something that can fit onto a finger and let you switch between different devices more easily?
That’s the promise that the Wearable Ring Controller by Prolo is making. Called the Prolo Ring, it is a Bluetooth wearable input controller that can be worn on your index finger. It has a trackpad that your thumb can use to move the cursor and scroll, and a touch strip that your other hand’s index finger can operate. The Pro Edition even supports air gestures, giving you another way to control your devices.
Designer: Prolo
The most noticeable design choice is its wide band. This gives your thumb room to work with an 18 × 30 mm capacitive touch surface rather than a tiny button. According to Prolo, the ring measures 23 mm wide and 2.9 mm thick and weighs between 4.1 and 5.2 grams. Its shell is made from polycarbonate, despite the metallic-looking finishes available for the Pro Edition. The broad profile makes it look more like a wearable tool than a discreet piece of jewelry.
That width also makes sizing important. Prolo lists US sizes 7–18 and requires test wear with its sizing kit or a 3D-printed sizer before you confirm your size. Your usual jewelry size may not translate directly to this wider band. Included adjustment shims help fine-tune a slightly loose fit. You can wear it on either index finger, keeping the trackpad facing your thumb.
The top touch strip, called the Modstrip, handles mode switching and additional commands. The four modes are Cursor, Navigation, Touch, and Air, organizing functions such as pointing, browsing, media playback, and motion gestures. Separating these controls lets the same small surface perform different jobs, although it also means learning which mode you’re using. Some interactions require both hands.
One particularly interesting feature is Joystick Assist. Swipe quickly from one edge of the trackpad to the other and keep holding, and the cursor continues moving. Moving your thumb farther from the center increases its speed; releasing stops it. This addresses the limited travel of a finger-sized trackpad, while ordinary trackpad movements remain available for finer positioning.
Switching devices uses a tap followed by a hold on the Modstrip. The ring disconnects from the current device and reconnects to another saved device, so “instantly” would be an overstatement. It connects to only one device at a time. For someone moving between a laptop and a tablet, the appeal is keeping the same controller rather than reaching for another one.
Basic controls use standard Bluetooth HID, the protocol used by compatible input devices, without requiring a dedicated driver or app. Prolo lists support for Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, and iOS/iPadOS, plus compatible smart TVs and XR devices. Available functions vary by device and app. It can also work alongside your existing mouse and keyboard rather than requiring you to replace them.
The Pro Edition adds more than 40 customizable gestures, assignable shortcuts, macros, and profiles. Prolo Studio, the free desktop companion app, handles customization. You could organize controls around presentations or media playback rather than use every available gesture. Push-to-talk can trigger dictation or AI shortcuts, but the ring has no microphone; a connected device handles the voice input.
Prolo claims up to 10 hours of typical use per charge and includes a magnetic charging cable. The ring is not waterproof, so it needs to come off before showering or swimming. For cramped workspaces, its clearest potential benefit is freeing you from needing a separate mousing surface. Whether that convenience outweighs wearing a broad band and learning its controls will depend on how you work.
results.summary:
The Prolo Ring is a new Bluetooth-enabled wearable input controller designed to replace traditional mice by allowing users to navigate multiple devices using finger-based gestures and touch surfaces.

### Key Points
- The Prolo Ring features an 18 × 30 mm capacitive trackpad and a "Modstrip" for switching between four distinct control modes.
- The Pro Edition supports over 40 customizable air gestures, macros, and shortcuts via the Prolo Studio desktop application.
- It connects via standard Bluetooth HID to Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, and XR devices without requiring specific drivers.
- The device weighs between 4.1 and 5.2 grams and offers approximately 10 hours of battery life on a single charge.
- Users must select from US sizes 7–18 using a provided sizing kit, as the 23 mm wide band requires a precise fit.

### Why it Matters
This wearable technology offers a space-saving alternative for professionals managing multiple devices in cramped workspaces by eliminating the need for a dedicated mouse surface. By consolidating input controls into a single finger-worn device, it provides a versatile, cross-platform solution for users who frequently switch between laptops, tablets, and smart TVs.

results.title: Will Voters Care About Max Miller’s Alleged Abuse?
results.author: Chris Heath
results.content:
This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
Just after 10:30 a.m. on the last Monday in September, Max Miller, the 37-year-old Republican congressman from Ohio, representing the state’s Seventh District, took a seat at a table in a conference room at the Hilton Cleveland Downtown hotel. He wore a white quarter-zip rugby sweatshirt — zip down, collar popped, sleeves rolled half up — and slouched, sometimes swiveling in his leather chair.
Until recently, Miller — a former Trump protégé, moderately effective in Congress — was little known outside Washington and Ohio. But over the past five months he’d entered the national stage through a series of alarming allegations. As he summarized in August: “I’ve been portrayed as an abusive husband, an abusive father, and a violent man.” His ex-wife, Emily Moreno, the daughter of Republican senator Bernie Moreno, had decided repeatedly not to press charges against him, but she’d accused Miller, in legal filings and police interviews, of throwing her against a wall, scalding her with boiling water, and holding a gun to her head. In the winter, Miller had been investigated after their 2-year-old daughter was discovered to have a broken collarbone. (The local prosecutor’s office found there was “insufficient admissible evidence” to support moving forward to a grand jury, and neither Miller nor anyone else was charged with a crime.)
Miller was at the Hilton to be deposed by his ex-wife’s lawyers, as a part of their ongoing dispute over their divorce settlement — Moreno was now fighting for full custody of their daughter. The accusations against him darkened the edges of the room.
Though on occasion he’d previously come across as a bit pompous and self-righteous when he talked about these matters in public, he’d always seemed to take the accusations as serious, denying them all, and to strive to project sincerity. But the Max Miller now, at the head of the long table of lawyers, three of his facing off against four of Moreno’s, presented as someone very different. At times he wore a contemptuous smirk. Flipping through court documents, he muttered, “There’s so much crap here.” Pressed to clarify a factual detail, he replied, “I don’t remember what I had for breakfast.” He often gave the impression he was above it all, as if this whole undertaking was ridiculous.
Whenever he chose, he would stonewall, sometimes finding five or six different ways of refusing to answer a direct question. Whenever he preferred to, he’d answer a “yes or no” question with a diatribe or an anecdote that he appeared to find satisfying or amusing. One that he seemed to particularly relish, overruling his lawyer’s efforts to quiet him, was his explanation for something he was alleged to have said while his wife was giving birth — that the experience was like “watching a playground being set on fire.” He insisted, grinning, that the words had come from a hospital nurse. Repeatedly, he insulted Moreno’s lawyers, referring to them as “savages” and “awful”; their line of questions, he said, half-smiling, was “so sadistic.”
At one point, he was asked a question that referred to something he’d allegedly said some weeks before in a courthouse hallway to one of Moreno’s lawyers. According to a filing, he’d told the man his fiancée was “not much of a looker” and “insinuated that she was a prostitute,” saying he could find women like her “on a street corner for $10.” At the Hilton, Miller was prompted to answer “yes or no” regarding the “not much of a looker” part, and leaped in with apparent glee: “That was in response to him saying … that my girlfriend was good at sucking cock.”
Miller had many times called his situation, and his ex-wife’s claims, “sad,” painting the experience as a painful ordeal. His recent legal filings had described the toll as “significant ongoing mental distress, fear, anxiety, emotional harm, and fear for safety, reputation, and parental rights.” But for much of that day in September, roughly a month from Election Day, Miller appeared to be having fun.
Miller is in many ways a middle-of-the-road Republican: He talks about minimizing taxes, increasing funding for law enforcement, and “securing” the southern border. He’s against Trump’s tariffs but defers to the president’s authority on the matter, has argued for guardrails on AI, and favors more legal immigration to combat population decline. In his next term, he’s said, he wants to push for a more diverse energy policy, including wind power, despite the president’s disdain for it.
His constituency is likewise red but moderate. Some of the biggest towns in his district — suburban and rural, from a swath of northeastern farmland up to Cleveland and the edge of Lake Erie — swung for Obama in his first presidential run. Miller won his seat comfortably in 2022 and 2024, and, according to the 2025 Cook Political Report’s partisan-voting index, the district currently leans Republican by five points. For Miller, the election on November 3 is most likely to hinge on what voters believe about his personal story.
Miller was born into a wealthy Ohio family whose fortune was made several generations before in forestry and real estate. After graduating from Cleveland State University in 2013, he joined the Marine Corps Reserves (he would serve for six years), and in 2015 he got his first foothold in politics after a cousin brokered an introduction to members of Marco Rubio’s presidential campaign. Miller subsequently pivoted to the Trump campaign and, after Trump’s victory over Hillary Clinton, became one of the cadre of young operatives in the first-term White House, eventually becoming a key advance man.
Questions about Miller’s personal behavior first made it to the press in 2018, when a Washington Post story about inexperienced and poorly vetted staffers in the Trump administration detailed Miller’s history of “assault, disorderly conduct, fleeing an officer and underage drinking,” pointing to a number of incidents including one in 2010, when he, at the age of 21, was arrested for fighting outside a Cleveland Heights hookah bar at around two in the morning, punching through a glass door and leaving a trail of blood from his wrist. Miller told the paper: “Growing up, everyone makes mistakes. Who I was in the past is not who I am now.”
He moved through various positions in the first Trump White House and, in 2020, pivoted to working on the reelection, becoming a deputy campaign manager. After Trump lost that November, Miller was appointed senior White House adviser for the remainder of the term, and in that role, he helped to make practical arrangements for the January 6, 2021, rally that preceded the attack on the Capitol. In his later testimony to the January 6 committee, he would call its investigation “an abuse of power,” but he was less combative than some. Miller had gone home 20 minutes into Trump’s speech on January 6, his job done, and he told the committee, “What happened on that day is horrific. People who broke the law and breached the Capitol should be held responsible and accountable … and unfortunately we will have to relive it every year and then teach our kids this day in history so they never forget it.”
Miller remained in Trump’s good graces, and in February 2021, Trump endorsed him in a primary challenge against Republican incumbent Anthony Gonzalez, who had voted to impeach the president. That June, when Trump reemerged from Mar-a-Lago seclusion to give his first Biden-era rally, he would do so in Wellington, Ohio, alongside Miller. There, Trump offered up a characteristically rambling elegy — “an incredible patriot … Max, great guy … a trusted aid of mine … he’s got a passion for this country like you wouldn’t believe” — and in return Miller told the crowd, “I have never had a greater role model than President Donald J. Trump.”
During his run for the House, Miller faced renewed scrutiny over who he was and had been. That July, Politico interviewed more than 60 people who had known him in his youth or in the White House, reporting that he was seen as a smooth political operator but also a “cocky bully.” Multiple former classmates from Shaker Heights High School said he was known for his anger: “He had a huge temper”; he was “a loose cannon”; “very belligerent” and “super-misogynistic.” Female classmates in particular described being “very uncomfortable” around him. The reporters relayed two stories of Miller allegedly assaulting women.
In the first, said to have taken place during high school at a party in his parents’ house, Miller was accused of pushing a girl out of his room so hard that she fell down a flight of stairs after she resisted his advances. In the second, an incident from 2020, he was alleged to have pushed his then-girlfriend, Stephanie Grisham, former Trump press secretary and the First Lady’s chief of staff, against a wall in their Washington apartment and slapped her in the face after she accused him of cheating. (Through a representative, Miller declined to participate in this story, and his team did not respond to multiple requests for comment. To Politico in 2021, lawyers for Miller said they “categorically” denied both assault allegations.)
At the time, none of what was alleged appeared to make any dent in Miller’s political prospects. The following year, he won the Republican primary and was elected a member of Congress. Miller was also a married man. In 2021, he’d started dating Emily Moreno, a Trumpworld acolyte about five years his junior, from another wealthy Cleveland-area family. Moreno’s Colombia-born father, Bernie, had made his money in car dealerships and as Miller campaigned for Congress, Bernie Moreno was campaigning for the Republican nomination for the Senate. (That time around, Moreno would drop out, but he would win Ohio’s other Senate seat in 2024.) Emily Moreno, meanwhile, had her own niche fame in the Republican sphere. In 2018, she’d launched a conservative dating app, DonaldDaters, for Republicans seeking refuge from “liberal intolerance.”
On August 27, 2022, Miller and his bride threw a wedding party hosted by Donald Trump at his Bedminster golf club. “The best part?” Miller’s new father-in-law posted on Facebook. “Watching the smiles on their faces and the love they have for each other in their eyes!” Their Williams Sonoma registry is still online: It appears they got most of what they asked for, though by the look of it, not the eight American-flag appetizer plates or the eight American-flag mugs. Both came into the marriage with money. (In their prenup, Miller listed a net worth of $6,423,873, the bulk of this in four family trusts. Moreno listed $122,500, but a 2023 House finance report showed she had assets worth millions.)
The following November, Moreno gave birth to their daughter. Just eight months later, in August 2024, Moreno left Miller, moving out with their child while Miller was away at work into a house she’d bought without his knowledge. Toward the end of the month, Miller formally filed for divorce.
Things turned ugly almost immediately. The following week, in an emergency motion for parenting time, Miller asserted that his wife was impeding access to his daughter “to gain leverage” in the divorce “and for personal financial gain.” He said that Moreno had refused to allow him to take their daughter overnight, citing, among other reasons, some unspecified drug use and a fear that he wouldn’t return the child. Miller called both ideas baseless and said he’d taken a drug test proving he was clean. In a retort, Moreno’s lawyers said she had “a great deal of concerns about her husband’s decision-making and personal life choices” and that she had “left the marital residence for her own security, safety and well-being and that of their infant daughter.”
By the end of September, Miller was demanding that both he and his wife undergo psychiatric testing and asserted that Moreno, whose behavior he described as “erratic and concerning,” had previously been diagnosed as bipolar, something he would repeat in various ways many times thereafter. He claimed he’d learned this secondhand from one of Moreno’s doctors and that Moreno had later “disclosed she was admitted into a hospital for mental health treatment.” (Moreno, who declined to comment for this story, has maintained that she was misdiagnosed.)
In January 2025, the couple agreed to a shared parenting plan, and that June, their divorce agreement was filed. Miller was to pay $2,500 a month for child support; Moreno kept most of the wedding gifts and the dining room set; he kept three pieces of what was described as the “Jackson Hole, Wyoming, artwork.” But if anyone involved believed the conflict was now behind them, they would be very wrong.
Other specifics related to the divorce remain far from settled. Few days pass without new legal filings. And though many of these are brief and procedural, plenty more are densely argued, combative ripostes; in many, the two challenge each others’ suitability as parents. In the past year and a half, there have been three other separate court cases between Miller and Moreno: one charging domestic violence, one defamation, and one a civil-rights abuse. The last two are ongoing.
When allegations against Miller first appeared in the news this past spring, no Republicans called for him to step down. But in early August, after months of silence, his senator father-in-law denounced Miller, saying he was unfit to serve, and in the following days, a handful of other prominent Republicans demanded that Miller resign, including Ohio’s junior senator, Jon Husted. (It was later reported that Miller, in retort, described Husted as “as entertaining as a two-by-four” and “as smart as a box of rocks.”) When the final deadline approached for ballot changes, according to CNN, top House Republicans asked Trump to step in; Trump declined to force Miller out.
As early voting opened in the first week of October, some kind of uneasy truce appeared to be in place. According to the New York Times, aides to the president had pushed unhappy Republicans to “quiet down” and likewise urged Miller to stop talking publicly about his “family drama.”
Miller’s opponent in the race, Democrat Brian Poindexter, is a 47-year-old father of three and union ironworker — a Bernie Sanders–endorsed populist. When he won the Democratic primary in May, it seemed unlikely he’d make it any further. But in early August, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee added him to its Red to Blue program; the seat was now flippable. Later that month, the Associated Press reported that a Democratic PAC, House Majority, had increased its intended ad buy in the district sevenfold to $7 million. As of mid-October, the race appeared to be a toss-up.
It was in the fall of 2021, as Miller was campaigning for the House for the first time, that Stephanie Grisham first spoke publicly about her allegations against him; it was during the press run for her memoir, I’ll Take Your Questions Now: What I Saw at the Trump White House. Like Miller, Grisham had transitioned from the 2016 Trump campaign to working in and around the White House, moving from communications director for the East Wing — the First Lady’s office — to her role as White House press secretary, a nine-month stint in which she never held a single press conference. She later became the First Lady’s chief of staff. On the evening of the January 6 insurrection, she was among the first senior staff members to resign, destroying her relationship with the Trumps and many of her former colleagues.
Miller wasn’t named in Grisham’s memoir, but his identity was clear, and on the day the book was released, the Washington Post published an op-ed by Grisham. In the Post, she claimed she told Melania Trump that the boyfriend (still unnamed) had gotten “physical” with her but that the First Lady had been unconcerned. She made basically the same claim about the president. He had previously blessed the pair with, in her words, “his stock compliment” — that they were right out of central casting. A few weeks after speaking to his wife, while traveling on Air Force One, as Trump told Grisham “how broken up” her ex was over their separation, she “confided the same story about the physical abuse,” she wrote. “I told the president that this ‘great guy’ had anger issues and a violent streak.” Trump, according to Grisham, expressed surprise but little else: “A White House staffer accused of assault by a woman whom the president knew and trusted? It didn’t even seem to register on the president’s radar screen as a concern.”
A few hours after the op-ed appeared online, Miller filed a defamation suit, applying for an injunction to bar Grisham from saying more, including an immediate injunction that would have prevented her from speaking further on the matter that day. The latter was denied, and that afternoon, during an interview with Jake Tapper on CNN, Grisham acknowledged that the unnamed abuser was Miller. Since their breakup, she said, she’d learned he had “a history of violence with other women.”
In his suit, Miller and his lawyers asserted that Grisham’s “salacious and heinous false accusations,” without specifying which parts they were referring to, did not appear in “her supposed ‘tell-all’ book.” But the memoir did include the allegation, made multiple times in different forms, that the boyfriend had been abusive. And Miller’s depiction in the book — by no means flattering — has never been legally challenged. Miller first appears in the memoir in a bizarre but benign context as Trump’s “Music Man,” the staffer whom the president and others would send for, Grisham writes, when he needed soothing and who would play some selection of Trump’s favorite songs—“Memory” from Cats, the Rolling Stones’ “You Can’t Always Get What You Want.” “‘Go get the Music Man,’ Trump would say when he got bored … with whatever or whomever he was dealing with, or felt a rage coming on, or he just needed to chill.” (Miller has tweeted proudly about the nickname.)
Grisham, who declined to comment for this story, eventually fell in love with the Music Man. “As our careers progressed (well, mostly mine, with me pulling him along),” she writes, “so did our relationship.” By 2020, the couple had “moved in together and become the owners of a wonderful dog. We were always together — always — and I thought that would never change.” Grisham writes that she brushed off early signs of Miller’s temper; then, during the first months of COVID, he became “completely erratic and angry.” She worried that a neighbor “offered” him cocaine and suspected something untoward with another new friend, a woman, but he dismissed her suspicions, she says, and “continually called me names.” Soon, Grisham writes, she found the boyfriend, in the middle of the night, in a scene that “involved him on our couch and on his phone FaceTiming with someone. His pants also seemed to be missing.”
Of the end of their relationship, she writes, “The months of what I felt were abuse and cruelty had taken their toll, and I was finally done. When I left the house, it was a chaotic scene in every sense of the word, and I will leave it at that.” According to the book, the final wrench was yet to come, when the boyfriend would refuse to hand over their dog, which had been given to her as a birthday present.
Miller’s defamation suit against Grisham carried on for nearly two years, each side firing hard at the other. In one filing, Miller asserted that Grisham had “threatened me that if I ended our relationship, she would make false allegations of criminal conduct against me to negatively impact my career.” Grisham’s team said Miller’s intent “was to silence his ex-girlfriend for his political and personal gain” and threw out what sounded like a fairly direct threat: “Ms. Grisham has never publicly described Plaintiff’s abuse … Obviously, should the matter proceed to trial, Ms. Grisham knows that she would have to publicly describe both Plaintiff’s abuse and the circumstances surrounding that abuse during both the discovery and trial phases.”
In August 2023, Miller withdrew the suit. The parties had reached a private settlement, the terms of which would not become public for another three years. Among other conditions, Grisham was required to pay Miller one dollar, and both sides agreed not to publicly disparage the other under penalty of hefty damages — $1 million per transgression. When asked about this settlement during a later, related legal proceeding, Miller said, “The most thing that I got out of it was not paying my attorneys tens of thousands of dollars to be in a frivolous lawsuit to defend myself … I believe I spent over $300,000 in litigation.” It was, of course, Miller who had brought the lawsuit in the first place.
Accusations of abuse in the Miller-Moreno home first broke into the public in April when TMZ reported that an injury the couple’s daughter suffered in February — a fractured clavicle — was being investigated by police. Miller had also obtained a restraining order against his ex-wife; in his petition he alleged “domestic violence” against him and “harm” to their daughter consisting, essentially, of Moreno’s “false” accusations of abuse by him. In the same filing, he ascribed the child’s injury to “third parties” and then, several pages later, alleged it was his “belief” that Moreno was to blame.
Lawyers for both parties spoke to TMZ, neither directly explaining their position on the child’s injury, both competing in condescension. “Mr. Miller,” one of Moreno’s attorneys said, “lives off a trust fund and has a well-documented history of using his wealth, lawyers, and the courts to bully his enemies.” They went on to echo Grisham’s lawyers, years before: “Ms. Moreno will not be intimidated or silenced.” Miller’s attorneys, in turn, said it was “very sad the Congressman’s ex-wife is still battling her demons and using TMZ as an outlet.” The next week, Miller hit the theme of mental illness again, telling the New York Post, “This is truly exhausting. I just want what’s best for my daughter. Please stop giving my previously diagnosed bipolar ex-wife so much attention.”
On May 7 the Daily Mail reiterated the story of the child’s broken bone, resurfaced Miller’s troubled history with Grisham, and reported that he was “accused of years of documented physical abuse against his ex-wife.” The article, said to be supported by court filings and three sources, described the event that Miller would go on to refer to as “the boiling water story,” which allegedly took place on June 9, 2024, a few weeks before Moreno left Miller. The paper described “the Congressman allegedly hurling a pot of boiling water at Emily during an argument inside their Ohio home, with some of the water striking her chest,” and included a photograph of Moreno displaying an arc of reddened flesh across her sternum.
It also recounted a second much more recent incident, from February 1: “Miller allegedly grabbed and struck Emily … during a custody exchange at his Ohio home, leaving bruises on her arm, elbow, and torso as the couple’s two-year-old daughter … looked on.” More photos of Moreno showed red marks on her arm and stomach. (The photos were credited to Moreno, but she has denied supplying them to the paper.)
Miller responded the same day with a series of 11 tweets, dismissing the article as “nothing but lies.” He said he had exculpatory material that he’d given the Daily Mail reporter but that had been ignored and posted an audio clip from what would turn out to be hours of secretly recorded conversations with Moreno following their separation. (In an email to the Daily Mail, his lawyer wrote that Miller had been “surreptitiously recording his interactions with Emily out of concern that she would make false allegations against him down the road if the divorce could not be settled amicably.”) In the extract posted by Miller that day, Moreno can be heard saying that Miller is a “very kind person” and that she does not believe he would ever hurt her physically — “but,” she says, “you have hurt me emotionally, immensely.”
Miller had been aware of the accusation about February 1 for some time — Moreno had first raised it during the police investigation into their daughter’s injury in a conversation at her new home in Westlake, a 15 minutes’ drive from Miller’s, on February 25.
In that evening’s interview with two Bay Village police officers, Moreno explained that she’d arrived at Miller’s house to take their daughter to a birthday party. It was Miller’s designated parenting time, but he’d agreed to the pickup, she said, then became evasive when it came to firming up the details. “So I was probably, like, annoying that day,” she tells the police. “I just kept saying like, What time can I pick her up?” When she got to Miller’s, she says, their daughter was still in her pajamas, which led to further tension. “He got mad because I think he thought I was criticizing him,” she says. “He got really upset because I was just taking away his parenting time. And he threw me into the wall and I fell on the ground.” She goes on without pause: “And we left and I was fine, and we went to the birthday party. It was fine.”
When the detectives asked exactly where this happened, Moreno described a space in the entryway to the house, drew the layout on paper, and, at their request, acted out precisely what happened — playing the part of Miller while her lawyer played her. When her lawyer suggested she show the investigators a related photo, Moreno demurred, saying she didn’t want it to leave her house. When the detectives asked why, she said, “I just feel like it doesn’t make sense. It doesn’t make sense … Like, I don’t tell anyone. My parents don’t even know.” There was something about the way she slipped into the present tense that seemed particularly sad. She went on: “I handled myself during my divorce. I got out of the house and I didn’t need any of it to be about anything else.”
“After all this happened,” she told the detectives, Miller was “very nice” to her and they started getting along again. They were managing co-parenting, and “it was trending very good for us.” Until “right now” — that is, until their daughter’s injury, which she said she’d discovered while she and her daughter were taking a bath. The Cleveland Clinic had called child protective services, noting that the child’s mid-right-clavicle fracture was accompanied by a bruise resembling a handprint. CPS, not Moreno, had called the police. Speaking to investigators, she said she was uncertain that it was Miller who hurt their daughter. She also said she did not want to press charges for Miller allegedly throwing her against the wall.
The next day, Miller was interviewed about their daughter’s injury at the Bay Village police station, accompanied by two lawyers. He said he didn’t know how his daughter got hurt and at times seemed to cast suspicion back on his ex-wife, suggesting that Moreno was overwhelmed and not up to the task of parenting. He claimed he once saw her “violently shake” the child. The police did not mention the February 1 allegation — that his wife said he’d thrown her against the wall — but it soon came to Miller’s attention and he returned to the police station the following week with a dossier of what he called “irrefutable evidence” that Moreno was “lying.”
His lawyers had gathered all the messages exchanged between the two parents over the few weeks following the injury — Miller and Moreno are required by the court to communicate through an app called OurFamilyWizard. The communication was civil, sometimes even friendly. Miller’s team also produced footage from his home’s Ring camera of February 1. First Moreno is seen arriving, briefly collecting the two dogs she and Miller share (one is the French bulldog Grisham considered hers, Gus), then leaving around six minutes later. On the way out, she can be heard talking to their daughter, then, as she enters the frame, calling out “bye” presumably to Miller as she walks away quickly. Her ex-husband, off-camera, says, “Love you. Love you, R—”; it’s not clear if both phrases are intended for their daughter. Moreno doesn’t turn or break her stride but gives her daughter the half-swallowed direction, “Say ‘bye.’” To the police, one of Miller’s lawyers described Moreno’s departure — around eight seconds long — saying, “These videos of her leaving in a quite joyous mood in my opinion are conclusive that she is a total liar. Nobody, had they been assaulted by their ex-husband, would have been in that kind of a joyous mood.”
Miller’s team also told the police that Miller’s girlfriend, Jaclyn Alatrash, had been in the house that day and denied that any violence had taken place. (Alatrash, an anesthesiologist with a sideline in competitive bodybuilding, had been dating Miller for just over a year at the time.) The lawyers provided a statement from Alatrash, one Miller would describe in a parallel court filing: “Unbeknownst to Respondent, my girlfriend, J.A., was present inside my home during the entire custody exchange. J.A. makes it a practice to remain out of sight at my home during custody exchanges with Respondent due to Respondent’s unpredictable, irrational, unhinged, and confrontational behavior.”
Eight days later, however, Miller returned again to the police station, this time with his daughter and Alatrash. They’d come, Miller said, to “do the right thing”: His lawyers had just noticed, reviewing video footage, that Miller’s girlfriend was not in fact present at the house that day.
It was one of many times Miller would overplay his hand, laying down claims with confidence, and often a fair amount of bluster and condescension, that would later fall apart. Whether it was intentional or not, he seemed to be used to getting away with things like this — a man accustomed to leaning on the world and it bending in his direction.
In mid-May, Miller sued Moreno for defamation. He once again posted on X, writing that the “false allegations” were “simply an attempt to destroy my personal and professional reputation.” He looked forward, he said, “to bringing the truth to light in court.”
It was in filings for this case, in defending herself, that Moreno’s firsthand account of the “boiling water” story became public. Of the June 2024 night in question, she wrote in an affidavit, “I told Congressman Miller that I was planning to leave him. He got extremely upset. He took hot water from a pan he had just cooked eggs in and threw it at me. Shocked, I fell to the floor and lay there in a fetal position. Congressman Miller took the sprayer from the sink and continued to spray me with hot water.” In his own affidavit, Miller argued essentially that “what actually occurred was horseplay,” and that it only involved water from the faucet — not the stove. (Miller’s lawyers would go on to refer to it as a “non-boiling, non-intentional sink-sprayer interaction.”)
The defamation case is still ongoing, and as it has proceeded, Moreno has never spoken directly to the press. Miller, meanwhile, has waged an intermittent but fairly aggressive public campaign throughout the summer. In early June, he spoke to the New York Post and shared another audio clip from the secretly recorded conversations. “The audio is key,” he told the paper. “She doesn’t know we have that audio. She doesn’t know that we have her admitting to her being bipolar.”
In a four minute and 47 second file, recorded at Moreno’s new home in late August 2024, five days before Miller filed for divorce, Moreno does acknowledge that she was once assessed as bipolar, though she disputes the diagnosis. She also holds firm to the idea that Miller abused her, a claim that at that point had been made only privately. “You’re gonna accuse me of abuse?” Miller asks, his tone both sardonic and slightly incredulous. “You are abusive,” she replies, steadfast. “It’s not an accusation.”
He moves on quickly to the question of evidence: “Okay,” he says, “so how are you gonna prove that I’m abusive?” When Moreno sighs in response, he goes on: “So this is your time for leverage. This is the time where you can get me to cave.” Moreno maintains her position, and Miller presses again: “But what do you have that you’re going to release that I’m abusive?”
She then refers to the water incident — “You poured steaming-hot water on me” — and says he’s been “insanely emotionally abusive.” She says she has photos with scars on her neck, photos he’s seen. Miller first appears to deny knowing what she’s talking about. “When you took the fucking faucet and poured it on my neck?” she says to him. He changes tack. “I never thought that that hurt you, and you know that,” he says.
Moreno eventually reminds him that she’d gone to her closet and the laundry room and cried, and that he’d cried too, repeating “I didn’t mean to hurt you” and “Why are you scared of me?” Miller eagerly grabs hold of what she has just said, as though it validated his point of view: “Yeah, I didn’t mean to hurt you! It wasn’t done with intent.” He brings this up repeatedly, as though her acknowledging that he’d said he didn’t want to hurt her absolves him of everything.
Toward the conversation’s end, he tries to again dismiss what happened as “playful.” When he argues that water from the sink never gets to burning temperatures, she tells him to check it when he gets home. He then reveals that he has already had his attorneys test this: “I figured that this is what you were going to come at me with.” He then makes yet another turn, seeming to accept that she was hurt: “There was no championing of it. There was no celebrating. I felt awful.” When he then presses her to confirm that he has “never touched” her “physically,” she asks him to leave.
All of this back and forth, it may be worth emphasizing, Miller decided to make public. He may have shared it with the Post because the conversation excluded mention of stove-boiled water. He may also have believed, just as he appears to do in the recording, that her acknowledgment of his perspective validates it. “You just admitted yourself,” he says at one point, “I didn’t mean to hurt you. That just came out of your own mouth.” “Yes, Max,” she replies, in the tone of a woman who’s had similar conversations before. “And that’s true — you do think that.”
Still, it seems clear from what Miller tells the Post, that he believes the public will recognize what kind of woman they’re dealing with. “It really shocks me,” he told the Post, “and it pains me too, that the mother of my child wants to be known as the next Amber Heard.”
The previous month, Moreno had submitted to the court a handwritten apology letter, in blue ink and all capital letters, from Miller, which she said he gave her immediately after the water incident. Miller countered that the letter was an expression of “general remorse” about the state of their marriage and came in direct response to a political argument with Moreno’s father, a fight that had caught his wife in the middle.
It’s a strange, vulnerable letter, the kind that no one writing would ever want to find an audience beyond its intended recipient, one that spirals into a final declaration of “I love you, even if you think I don’t. I love you so much. I’m so sorry. I’m just a fuck up and worthless.” This, too, is another, very different Max Miller.
“My entire life I have struggled with personal relationships,” he writes. “I seem to always do well professionally, but then my personal life is in shreds … Like you feel, I’m scared and crushed. There is nothing more important in my life than you and our daughter R—. I failed to do that and I now have to live with that. I don’t know what to do. I do know you love me, protect me and care for me. I failed to do that for you … I just want to close my eyes and wake up and everything be normal. I know that won’t happen. I’m sorry I failed you and R—. It’s eating me alive.”
On June 10, CNN reported that it had obtained video footage of Moreno’s late-February conversation with the Bay Village police. In it, Moreno had described Miller holding a gun to her head.
CNN aired only a portion of the footage — it was effectively audio, the whole frame blacked out. In the complete tapes, the couple’s daughter, 2 years old, can be heard somewhere in the distance, playing with Moreno’s mother.
As Moreno is interviewed by Detective Kelly Rhoades and Detective Sergeant Ed Chapman about her daughter’s injury, she does not proactively bring up any abuse she herself has faced. But deep into the nearly two-hour conversation, couched as their final question before they leave, the detectives mention disclosures Moreno made to CPS. Would she like to talk about any of that? Initially she declines, but when her lawyer gently presses — “If there is anything you would like to say, I think now would be the time” — she begins.
“I already said,” she tells them, “I think sometimes Max gets angry.” Rhoades, the female officer, has been leading the interview; “Has he ever hurt you?” she asks. If Moreno gives a verbal response, it isn’t audible, but Rhoades seems to take some sign of assent.
“I was just scared of him a lot,” Moreno says eventually. “And that’s why I left the house and I moved out.” Haltingly, retreating a few times to the idea that Miller “just gets really mad,” she explains that he was often angry specifically about the baby crying — that he would want her to make it stop — and then she says plainly, as if it were an incidental detail, “I know there was a few times when I would have to change the diaper and he’d have his gun on me.”
Moreno tells the investigators it’s embarrassing to talk about, but with their encouragement, she proceeds to describe one such incident. She says that in January 2024, she told Miller she wanted to leave and then backs up to New Year’s Eve 2023. Late that night, she says, he held a gun to her head in the bedroom. He’d been upset with her — she didn’t remember exactly why, but “the baby’s yelling, I’m doing everything wrong, and he just wants quiet because he works really hard.” At the time, the baby slept in a bassinet at their bedside; Miller didn’t like that, she says, “because he liked to watch TV.” When Moreno needed to change the baby, she turned the lights on, and, she says, Miller began to yell. Rhoades asks what he did with the gun, and Moreno seems to want to say as little as possible: “Holds it on me.”
She says she told her therapist about it at the time. The detectives ask if she wants to make a formal report, but as with the wall incident, she declines. “No one’s going to believe me,” she says. Rhoades tells her this isn’t true. “I feel,” Moreno replies, clearly pushing out these words through tears, “like I was just set up.” She’d loved her job in D.C. and then Ohio had been “good for a really long time” too. But “slowly, it just became like I was an island … I wasn’t allowed to talk to my friends. He told me my family hated me.” The physical abuse, she eventually says, had begun just before they were married.
In an interview with CNN’s Lauren Fox, Miller denied he’d ever held a gun to his wife’s head or ever done anything similar. He did not have, he said, “a weapon that’s even easily accessible in my home like that.” He “absolutely” had weapons, he went on, but they were always locked away. The details of a separate recent legal battle, in which Miller alleged antisemitic harassment by a local doctor — an incident that played out between the two men’s cars, on the highway — suggests that Miller carries a gun on him, at least outside the home: He said he’d held his gun on his lap, ready, should it be needed.
In early July, Stephanie Grisham sued Miller for breach of contract — for breaking their 2023 settlement agreement by disparaging her in public. In the secretly recorded audio clip Miller had posted on X in May, during his torrent of posts defending against the allegations in the Daily Mail, Moreno could be heard describing Grisham’s past accusations against Miller as “wrong” and “evil.” On X, Miller characterized the clip, writing, “@MsEmilyMoreno admits … everything alleged by Stephanie Grisham was fabricated.” Setting aside the logical issue that Moreno was not in a position to “admit” that Grisham’s account was untrue, Miller seemed to be calling Grisham a liar.
In court later in the summer, Miller, on the witness stand virtually from Washington, would contend that, whatever he had or hadn’t done, Grisham had violated their agreement first. He cited her own earlier activity on X, a post beginning “Today I feel broken over what so many men with money & power get away with. Over & over & over.” She’d posted it the same day TMZ had broken the story of Miller’s child-abuse allegations and reposted it the day of the Daily Mail report. (Grisham claims she was talking about other men, especially Jeffery Epstein.) As for his own tweet, in what seemed a bold and borderline nonsensical move, Miller blamed his aides, saying he hadn’t had his social-media passwords for two years and that nothing under his name on any social platform could be assumed to be his own words. (He also called “Twitter … insignificant,” “a sideshow,” and “a circus.”) It was, however, on X that Miller had made some of his most robust arguments in his own defense and against Moreno and Grisham.
On August 2, a Sunday, he did so again, taking to the platform to host a livestream — to make what he called a “very genuine” appeal. He wanted to be unmediated by journalists, who had been of no use to him. In a nearly 20-minute monologue, he addressed the story of his daughter’s broken collarbone, saying that CPS had investigated and found him “not guilty.” (In fact, it had found the claim against him “unsubstantiated,” and the local prosecutor had not brought charges against Miller or anyone else.) Miller also noted another incident, previously unfamiliar to the public, that he said had been investigated in January 2025: He said there had been an earlier injury to his daughter — he didn’t specify what kind — and that workers at his daughter’s day care had ultimately been found responsible. The public record on this is unclear; we know only that Miller brought a lawsuit against Nest schools in February 2025, alleging quite serious physical and psychological harm to the child. (Earlier this year, the parties reached a settlement agreement and the case was dismissed.)
It was on this livestream that Miller most forcefully denied Moreno’s allegation regarding the gun, calling it “absolutely outrageous.” He sounds self-assured, seeming to want to present himself as a dignified truth-teller. Even so, Miller more than once confuses key bits of information. He claims, for example, that Moreno invited him over “for dinner and to stay the night” two days after the alleged gun incident, though the two were still married and living together at that time. He also describes the couple’s divorce as “amicable” and gives an incorrect date (off by six months) for when they were divorced. Toward the end of the livestream, Miller announced that he was publishing a Dropbox full of relevant material: It was a massive data dump of edited court documents and transcripts, 17 audio recordings, five videos — all selected to substantiate his side of the story.
If Miller imagined that any of this would calm the waters, he badly miscalculated. Within the hour, Senator Bernie Moreno, who had not yet spoken publicly on any element of his daughter’s legal battles, issued an extraordinary public statement. “The last two years,” he wrote, “have been pure hell.” He had hoped to keep “the matter” private, he said, “out of concern for the safety” of his family, “but Max Miller’s increasingly erratic and dangerous behavior has made that impossible.” Miller, he wrote, had admitted privately to needing “serious psychological help”: “He is a danger to my daughter, and I hold my breath every minute he has custody of my granddaughter. If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them. He should not serve in the House of Representatives.”
The next day, Monday, Trump phoned Miller to talk about his campaign. Election Day was now three months away. According to Miller, as he told it later on CNN, Trump said, “Maxie, it’s going to be a tough race,” and “I don’t know if you’re going to be able to pull this one out.” Miller told the president he had no plans to step aside.
The next morning, news broke of potential “child sexual abuse material” in Miller’s Dropbox. It was an allegation from Moreno’s lawyers, who’d found images of Miller and Moreno’s daughter, at least one of which, they said, could be considered illegal. (The picture was one Moreno had sent to Miller when she found the handprint-like bruise in February.) Miller’s attorney Aaron Minc took responsibility for the mistake. Moreno’s lawyers would soon file a federal civil-rights lawsuit on behalf of the couple’s daughter, accusing Miller and Minc of having “recklessly published and disclosed to the world a nude image of the child depicting her genitalia.” (That case is still ongoing. Miller’s attorneys have requested it be dismissed on various technical grounds.) The Dropbox included an audio file — another of the secretly recorded conversations with Moreno — in which Moreno says to Miller, “I’m sure you record all our conversations.” Miller replies, “No, I don’t.”
On that same Tuesday morning, Bernie Moreno, exiting a closed office and attempting to make his way down a Senate corridor, was surrounded by reporters. Miller had posted a reply to the senator’s written statement, addressing him directly, saying, in part, “You know this isn’t true and the only reason you are speaking out now is to hide from your own media circus.”
Especially to those following the evolving news of the scandal, this sounded like a veiled threat. Roughly two weeks before, in a lengthy story on Miller’s past and present, Mother Jones had reported a threatening text message, found in an April court filing, that Miller had sent to Bernie Moreno. “I’m sick of this,” Miller had written. “You know I never hurt our daughter. Take this however you want, everyone is going to get to know you better than your wife does. Enjoy the ride brother, I wouldn’t have to do this if you could keep your lying daughter under control.”
Some commentators believe Miller was alluding to an allegation about Moreno’s personal life that first surfaced in the winter of 2024, when, following a data breach, the Associated Press found that Moreno’s email account was used to create a men-for-men profile on Adult Friend Finder years before, in 2008. (Moreno has claimed that this was the result of a prank.) If Miller’s intimation referred to something political, Miller and Moreno do not seem to have clashed publicly about politics. Moreno was reputedly anti-Trump for many years, once likening listening to Trump to “watching a car accident that makes you sick,” though he has recently become as stalwart a Trump supporter as Miller.
Now, stopped unhappily before the Senate’s gold and granite elevators, Moreno shook his head. “It’s the ramblings of a madman,” he said, referring to the “media circus” comment. What his family was experiencing was “truly the seventh level of hell.” He explained that until now his daughter had asked him not to speak publicly: She would be tied to Miller, through their child, for the rest of her life. “My daughter,” he said, nodding, as if shaking off a restraint, “lives in constant fear of this man. Not like something that’s existential, but deeply in her heart. She fears what this guy is capable of. You can’t fathom what that makes me feel like.” When Moreno raised his hand to signal he was done, the questions kept coming, and he eventually described picking up his granddaughter from Miller’s custody the previous weekend. His former son-in-law, he told the reporters, had refused to hand over the child’s little blue bunny, the stuffed animal she sleeps with, and “held it hostage for 48 hours.” In the following days, Mother Jones would report emails and text messages suggesting Miller had done this before.
Within an hour, the House Committee on Ethics announced it would be investigating if Miller “may have engaged in domestic violence and abuse or illegal drug use”; Miller announced that he’d requested this “to clear my name from these horrific attacks on myself and family.” (This investigation is ongoing.)
That afternoon, Miller made a calamitous appearance on The Lead With Jake Tapper, beginning with a question about whether the congressman had really been holding a blue bunny hostage. To that, Miller offered a curious kind of deflection. “If that were true,” he said, “that would be incredibly disturbing” — then shifted to criticizing his ex-father-in-law, noting how long it had taken him to speak out. Before long, Miller was complaining to Tapper about how little of his interview with Lauren Fox earlier that summer had aired alongside the network’s bombshell report about the gun. Miller said he’d played for Fox “three separate audio videos” of his daughter saying “I do not want to go to Mommy’s,” “I do not want Mommy’s,” and “I do not feel safe.”
That offered Tapper a perfect pivot to a subject it seemed he’d been planning to raise. After reiterating details from February’s suspected child-abuse incident — “that the child-protection team says that your child had a right-clavicle fracture and, quote, ‘a bruise that accompanies the injury that appears to be in a handprint and appears to have been inflicted,’ unquote” — he challenged Miller to respond to his ex-wife’s claims to police that in the days before the broken collarbone was discovered, their daughter had told Moreno “Daddy kill you.” Their daughter had also told Child and Family Services, Tapper went on, “Daddy angry” and “Daddy’s house is scary.”
Moreno’s account of the moment when her daughter first said “Daddy kill you” is also from her interview with the Bay Village detectives. On Sunday, February 15, she had gone over to Miller’s house because their daughter was out of sorts, “just really upset,” in a way that seemed “very out of the ordinary.” When the police ask Moreno to explain, she says, “I don’t know how to say it … she just wasn’t like … coming back to life.” (She would later test positive, a “really faint line,” in Moreno’s account, for strep, but without a fever.) Moreno tried to revive her daughter with some of her favorite foods— yogurt with dried strawberries, egg, sausage — but she wasn’t interested. Only when Moreno brought out her interactive Larry the Monster book did the child perk up a little. According to Moreno, it was then that her daughter said the words, in front of both her and Miller, “Daddy kill you, Daddy kill you.” Moreno tells the investigators that Miller immediately said, “I swear I don’t know where she heard that.”
When Tapper mentioned the phrase “Daddy kill you” to Miller, his response was a feeble one on several levels. “Jake,” he began, seeming to gather up the earnestness required. “I wish you could talk to my beautiful baby girl. She can’t string together sentences like that. She’s 2 and a half years old. She doesn’t have the ability to articulate any of what you just said. That is an entire fabrication of the truth.”
Tapper retorted, firm and prosecutorial, “You just told me that she was scared to go to Mommy’s house … But now you’re saying she’s not capable of saying ‘Daddy kill you’?” Miller’s position was further undermined by the tranche of OurFamilyWizard messages — the same tranche Miller had given to the police to prove how well he and Moreno were getting on and that he had just shared publicly in his Dropbox.
On February 16 — the day after their daughter first said these disturbing words, as Moreno tells it — Moreno sent Miller a FamilyWizard message just before eight in the evening: “She said the same comment again that she said in front of us yesterday, so I feel obligated to ask. ‘Daddy kill you.’ Any idea where she picked that up or overheard it.” Miller replied one minute later: “There is no way she is saying that, the only time I heard that was with you the other day.”
In the first half of October, Trump twice held rallies in Ohio. At the first, on October 3 in Montgomery County, in the southwestern corner of the state, Miller was not present and not mentioned, even though his was exactly the kind of tight race Trump was supposedly there to influence. A spokesperson for Miller was quoted in the New York Times claiming that Miller had been invited but had been unable to attend. When Trump returned nine days later to rally in Youngstown — in the northeast, much closer to Miller’s territory — Miller was there, though relegated to the crowd, while Husted and Bernie Moreno were among the opening speakers. Toward the end of Trump’s speech, he mentioned Miller alongside other local candidates. The fact that he did so was widely reported as a renewed public endorsement, but it was nothing like his previous tributes: “And Congressman Max Miller, who’s here. Thank you, Max, for coming. Thank you. Very good. Thank you.”
In recent weeks, it seems that Miller has tried to avoid making the news. He’s skirted reporters on the steps and in the halls of the Capitol, ignoring their questions and spouting statistics about his congressional achievements as he walks on — “Did you know that we’ve returned, I think, over $50 million to our district, back to our community?” — looking smugly satisfied.
But in the middle of October, Miller dropped a new TV ad that addressed his personal life. “Too many of us know the pain of divorce,” he begins and summons a soulful stare into the camera. He says his “family’s heartbreak” has been dragged into the public arena “because that’s politics.” Before the camera slowly pans over a selection of hand-drawn Father’s Day cards, he claims that “despite relentless press and allegations, every allegation against me was proven false.”
This is untrue. While neither he nor anyone else was found at fault in the investigation of his daughter’s broken collarbone, none of the allegations of assault against Moreno or Grisham has ever been formally investigated.
Recently, Miller appears to be taking only softball interviews, though he still sometimes trips himself up. In one video appearance, he sat in front of a photo of himself and Trump, signed by the president, reeling off his achievements, as though everything was going to plan. Then, smiling into the camera, he briefly addressed his personal woes, offering reassurance. “The truth,” he said, “is so much different than the reality of the situation.”
results.summary:
Republican Congressman Max Miller of Ohio is facing intense public scrutiny and a competitive reelection bid following a series of serious domestic abuse allegations from his ex-wife.

### Key Points
- Max Miller, a former Trump aide, is currently embroiled in multiple legal disputes, including ongoing domestic violence, defamation, and civil rights lawsuits involving his ex-wife, Emily Moreno.
- Allegations against Miller include claims of physical assault, such as throwing his ex-wife against a wall and scalding her with hot water, as well as holding a gun to her head.
- The House Committee on Ethics has launched an investigation into whether Miller engaged in domestic violence or illegal drug use.
- Miller has denied all allegations, characterizing them as politically motivated, and has faced public condemnation from his former father-in-law, Senator Bernie Moreno.
- Despite the controversy, Miller remains in a tight race against Democratic challenger Brian Poindexter for Ohio’s Seventh District seat in the November 3 election.

### Why it Matters
The scandal has transformed a previously safe Republican seat into a toss-up, forcing national party leaders to navigate the political fallout of Miller’s personal conduct. The situation highlights the intersection of private legal crises and public office, testing the limits of party loyalty and voter tolerance for candidates facing severe character allegations.
